source_data.original_text:
In gently undulating pasture, on the E side of the summit of a low broad ridge. A circular flat-topped mound (diam. 12.6m at base, 8m at top) surrounded by a fosse (Wth 2.4m at base) and an external earth and stone bank (Wth 5.6m; int. H 1.05m; ext. H 0.3m). The mound rises 1.35m above the base of the fosse. Recorded in 1836 as 'Sídheán a'Gháire' (OSL, 423), a translation of which was given in Wood-Martin (1887-8, 269) as 'the Fairy Mount of Laughter'. A bowl-barrow (SL033-050----) lies c. 50m to WSW.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

This ring-barrow was severely damaged by land reclamation work in April 2006: the enclosing bank was levelled, the fosse infilled and several pits dug through the central mound. A rescue excavation (06E0720) was undertaken over three weeks in August 2006 by Margaret Keane, National Monuments Service (Keane 2009, 469, no. 1770). The excavation concentrated on the western side of the crest of the mound, and in addition a single trench was excavated across the fosse and external bank. The excavation of the fosse revealed that it was originally c. 2.5m wide at the top and c. 0.9m deep, with a sharply cut external edge, a rounded base, and a shallower profile on the internal mound side. A single post-hole was recorded just inside the edge of the mound crest. On the crest of the mound, the upper deposits consisted of spreads of charcoal-rich soils, with burnt bone and occasional artefacts interleaving with a spread of compact white/grey silt. Burnt material spread across the site may represent rakings of funeral pyre material. Beneath these layers, were a cluster of eight pits (max. dims. 0.3-1.3m) filled with deposits of burnt bone, in a clayey matrix with occasional artefacts. The interior edges of some of the pits were significantly charred. The most impressive pit (D c. 0.5m) had a basal deposit of cremated bone, and upper fills rich in charcoal and burnt bone. Artefacts recovered include ten glass beads or bead fragments, two unperforated glass beads/toggles, a single copper alloy spiral ring, five copper alloy pins, a copper alloy rod, copper alloy fragments, iron fragments, pieces of slag, worked flint and chert. (Keane 2009, 469, no. 1770). 

Date of revised upload: 10 March 2016

In low-lying gently undulating wet pasture. A slightly raised circular area (33m E-W) defined by an earth and stone bank (Wth 4.25m; int. H 0.55m; ext. H 1.6m) W-NW and by a scarp NW-SE. Elsewhere the enclosing element has been entirely quarried away. An external fosse (D 0.55m; Wth 1.6m at base) survives W-N and is evident N-E as a dark band of grass. The interior is quarried away except for a band of between 7 and 9m inside the surviving bank and scarp. An E-W road lies c. 8m to S of the present limits of the rath. Indicated as a small embanked circular area (diam. c. 18m) on the 1838 OS 6-inch map; only the N half is indicated by arcs of hachures NW-NE on the 1941 OS 6-inch map.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In pasture, on a slight W-facing slope. This rath is not visible at ground level. It is depicted on the 1838 OS 6-inch map as an embanked circular enclosure (diam. c. 30m) and on the 1941 OS 6-inch map as a circular raised area (diam. c. 40m). It was described during a previous inspection in 1985 (SMR (1989) file) as an irregular oval earthwork defined by a bank NE-NW and by a scarp NW-NE. A fosse and a low outer bank were noted along the S arc. The interior was described as uneven with a rise in the W half.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on top of a ridge with excellent views in all directions. A roughly circular cairn (18m N-S; 20.6m E-W; max. H 1.40m) of grass-covered limestone stones. The cairn has been extensively disturbed at the centre and in the NW quadrant giving it an irregular appearance. Traces of a 'probable fosse' were noted along the N edge during a previous inspection (pers. comm. M. Keane and J. Farrelly). A large split slab (3.2m x 1.65m; T 0.65m) of weathered limestone lies flat near the NE edge. This stone is known locally as the 'Split Dolmen' or the 'Giant's Grave'. A second smaller slab (0.75m x 0.8m; T 0.2m) protrudes at an angle of c. 45 degrees from the cairn material to E of centre.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In pasture near the top of an E-facing slope. An oval area (int. diam. 30m E-W; 21m N-S) enclosed by two earthen banks with an intervening fosse (Wth 5m). The inner bank (Wth 2.5m; int. H 1m; ext. H 2m) is the most substantial. The outer bank (Wth 1.8m; ext. H 0.2m) has a gap (Wth 2m) at N. The entrance is through the inner and outer banks (Wth 3m and 4m respectively) at E with a causeway across the fosse, in line with a NE-SW field boundary which crosses the centre of the interior. A possible megalithic tomb (SL033-166----) lies c. 20m to W.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a gentle NNE-facing slope. A raised oval area (18m N-S; 14m E-W) defined by the footings of a stone wall (int. H 0.2m; ext. H 0.25; Wth at top 1.2m) SSE-NW and by a rocky scarp (H 1.75m) elsewhere. The footings of the wall are now grass covered and difficult to distinguish because of the generally rocky nature of the site. The N half of the interior is raised to compensate for the hillslope. The interior is undulating due to the presence of grass-covered rocks, clear of overgrowth and slopes gently down to NNE. The interior is said to have been used as a children's burial ground (SL033-045001-). One of four forts (see SL033-087001-; SL033-188001- and SL033-188002-) referred to in this townland in 1836 (OSNB vol. 1, 404-5).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In gently undulating pasture, on a slight W-facing slope. A large roughly circular dome-shaped mound (36m N-S; 40m E-W) defined by a fosse and an external earthen bank. The fosse (Wth 4.1m at base; Wth 8.95m at top) is evident all round and is densely overgrown and inaccessible E-W. The bank (int. H 0.85m to base of fosse; ext. H 1.1m) is evident all round, is incorporated into the field boundary system SE-SW and is densely overgrown and inaccessible E-W. The apex of the domed mound is slightly off-centre to S and is 4.1m higher than the top of the fosse. A disused quarry is situated outside the bank at NNE. This barrow appears to be formed around a natural hillock that has been modified to create a large earthwork. A ring-barrow (SL033-048----) lies c. 60m to SW and another (SL033-199----) c. 150m to SW.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In undulating pasture, on a N-facing slope and within a field system (SL033-070----). A rectangular area (11.5m N-S; 16m E-W) enclosed by an earthen bank (Wth 3m; int. H 0.2m; ext. H 0.4m) with an external fosse (Wth 3m). A possible entrance (Wth 2m) is on the W side. There is a quarry to S. This is the only moated site which lies within the substantial holdings in South Sligo belonging to the Cistercian Abbey at Boyle in Co. Roscommon (Carville 2002, 348-9 and 328-9) and therefore it could possibly be a moated grange belonging to the abbey.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In undulating rocky pasture on a slight WSW-facing slope and within a field system (SL033-070----). The enclosure lies above a sharp fall of ground on its N side and abuts a natural cliff (H 2.5-3.5m) to S. A slightly raised pentagonal area (38m N-S; 35m E-W) defined by an earth and stone bank (int. H 0.3m; ext. H 0.5m) SW-NNE. The bank (int. H 0.5m; ext. H 3.8m including the height of the natural slope) lies on the crest of a natural break of slope NW-N. A low earth and stone field boundary lies on the approximate line of the enclosure bank NNE-SE. From SE-SW, the limit of the enclosure is defined by an E-W orientated natural cliff which rises 2.5-3.5m above the interior. From SW-NW the bank consists of large limestone rocks (c. 0.5m x 0.5m x 0.3m) spaced 2-4m apart with earth and stone in between. These large rocks are not visible NW-NNE where the bank is purely of earth and stone. The interior is under grass, clear of overgrowth, slopes gently down to WSW and the W portion is slightly raised to compensate for the hillslope.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In rocky pasture, on a gentle S-facing slope 4m to the S of a cliff-face (H 2m). A circular area (4m N-S; 4.1m E-W) defined by an earth and stone bank (int. H 0.4m; ext. H 0.25m). The bank consists of rubble limestone covered by earth and moss and is best preserved on either side of the entrance where it is contained within two parallel rows of upright limestone slabs. These slabs also survive sporadically along the inner face of the bank, especially along the S arc. The bank is eroded and lower WSW-N. The entrance (Wth 0.85m) is at ENE and is lined with vertical limestone slabs. The interior is level and clear of overgrowth and is raised at S to compensate for the underlying natural slope and is slightly lower than the external ground level at N.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In rocky undulating pasture on a slight S-facing slope and incorporating a natural semicircular cliff-edge on its N side. A roughly circular area (16m N-S; 15m E-W) defined by an earth and stone bank (int. H 0.3m; ext. H 0.9m) E-WSW and by a natural curving cliff-edge (H 8-10m at N) WSW-E. Immediately outside the base of the bank E-WSW is a discontinuous line of upright limestone blocks and slabs (average dims. H 0.75m; Wth 0.55m; T 0.55m). These could be the remains of low stone walling or a revetment for the bank. The entrance is at S with a stony ramp to exterior. The width of the ramp (max. Wth 5m; min. Wth 2m) decreases as it rises into the interior. The interior is undulating and clear of overgrowth and is slightly raised on the S side to compensate for the hillslope. The cliff-edge fort lies within a field system (SL033-070----). An enclosure (SL033-057----) lies c. 50m to S.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In undulating rocky pasture, on the E side of a cliff and within a field system (SL033-070----). A slightly raised roughly pentagonal area (18m N-S; 14m E-W) defined by an earth and stone bank (int. H 0.2m; ext. H 0.4m) on the N, E and S sides. A vertical cliff (H 2m) defines the W side of the interior. The cliff changes direction, at an oblique angle, from a NNW-ESE orientation to a NE-SW orientation at W giving the interior its pentagonal shape. The earth and stone bank has a discontinuous outer facing of upright limestone slabs on the N and half of the E side. There are many small gaps (Wth 0.7-1m) through the bank. The interior is undulating and clear of overgrowth. To SE of centre is a weathered rectangular limestone block (L 0.9m; Wth 0.7m; H 0.65m; long axis E-W) with possible packing-stones under its N side. A denuded relict earth and stone field boundary (L 16m, oriented ENE-WSW) abuts the NE corner of the fort. This field boundary is visible in an aerial photograph (IASAP, 3043028-9) where it is seen to turn to the N c. 20m from the fort towards a cliff-edge fort (SL033-056----) c. 50m to N. Another relict boundary visible in the same photograph abutting the SW corner of the fort is not visible at ground level.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In undulating pasture, extending across an extensive area (c. 1.2km x 1km) of rocky limestone pasture. A system of relict fields, enclosed by low denuded earthen banks and stone walls, is evident. The field system is sinuous and of no regular pattern. The S portion consists primarily of earth and stone banks with or without associated fosses. In the SE corner is a pentagonal field (20m N-S; 22m E-W) defined by an earth and stone bank (int. H 0.35m; ext. H 0.45m) with an external fosse (D 0.4m) or drain on the NE, SE, SW and NW sides. The N side is defined by a WSW-ENE relict field bank (int. H 0.65m) with a relict drain (D 0.7m) on its N side. A short stretch of a relict field bank abuts it at S. The remains of a five-roomed rectangular house (c. 3m N-S, c. 19m E-W) (SL033-060002-), with low earth and stone walls, is adjacent to the NW corner of this field. Immediately to SW of the pentagonal field is a wedge-shaped field (19m NE-SW; Wth 7.6m W end; Wth 5m E end) defined by an earth and stone bank (int. H 0.3m; ext. H 0.8m) on all sides with an external fosse (D 0.45m) on the W, N and part of the S sides. The fosse kinks around the S side of an adjacent two-roomed rectangular house (SL033-060004-). Similar small relict fields are visible to E and SE. 
In the N portion of the field system, in the vicinity of a cliff-edge fort (SL033-196----), is a series of low drystone walls extending across an extensive area of outcropping limestone. Numerous monuments occur within the field system including a cashel and souterrain (SL033-067001; SL033-067002-), two raths (SL033-061----; SL033-066----), two cliff-edge forts (SL033-056----; SL033-058----), a moated site (SL033-053----), a rectangular enclosure (SL033-060003-), a hut site (SL033-196----) and several enclosures (SL033-054----; SL033-057----; SL033-197----).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In undulating pasture, in a slight natural depression on the top of a hill. There are excellent views in all directions except towards a hill at WNW. A circular raised area (15m N-S; 15m E-W) defined by an earth and stone bank (int. H 0.4m; ext. H 0.9m) NNE-W and by a scarp elsewhere. The interior is clear of overgrowth and is undulating, possibly due to quarrying; a quarry hole (4m N-S; 2m E-W; D 0.4m) is evident to N of centre. A dump of earth and stone (2m x 2m; H 0.3m) was noted against the internal face of the bank at S. A now disused field drain has been cut against the external face of the bank E-S and sections of a disused field boundary abut the external face of the bank at S and E. While there is no evidence of an internal fosse, the diameter and the location of this site suggest it is a ring-barrow.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

raw_items.raw_text: RICHARD FLEMING WHO MADE THIS IN THE YEARE 1712

source_data.original_text:
In undulating pasture, on a low rise with excellent views in all directions. A roughly circular raised area (35m N-S; 33m E-W) defined by two earth and stone banks with an intervening fosse. The interior is enclosed by an inner bank (int. H 0.45m; ext. H 3.9m); the width and internal height (H 1.8m) of the bank have been increased NNW-N to accommodate an OS trigonometrical station (now gone but indicated on the 1941 OS 6-inch map). The entrance (Wth 6m) is at E with breaks in the inner and outer banks and a ramp and causeway across the fosse. The fosse is evident all round with a slight infilling visible W-NW as a result of livestock traffic into the interior. The outer bank (int. H 1.05m; ext. H 0.7m) is evident NE-NNW; elsewhere it has been replaced by a drystone-built wall. There is a gap (Wth 2.2m) at W. A drystone-built wall has been constructed on the external edge of the top of the outer bank WSW-NW and an E-W earth and stone field boundary abuts the external base of the outer bank at S.
The interior is level and under grass with some hawthorn bushes. In the S half is a circular earthwork surrounded by a stone wall; on top of the enclosing bank on the S side of the earthwork is a stone monument of the Fleming family. The circular earthwork consists of a slightly raised level area (diam. 7.5m) enclosed by an earth and stone bank (H 0.3m). The earthwork is enclosed by a circular drystone wall (H 0.85m; T 0.65m) of rubble limestone with an entrance (Wth 1.6m) at N. The rubble limestone on the W side of the entrance is stone faced and coursed while the E side has mostly collapsed.
The Fleming monument (Flynn 2003-4, 22-3) consists of a rectangular column (0.75m N-S; 0.9m E-W; H 1.2m) of rubble limestone, mortared in rough courses. At the top of the N-facing side are two roughly shaped rectangular sculpted stones, both of similar dimensions (H 0.37m; Wth inscribed face 0.23m; T 0.45m). The westernmost stone is decorated with a stag, a heart between a unicorn and another animal as well as a hand holding a sword, a fleur-de-lys and an open hand. The easternmost stone is inscribed with capital letters in relief and reads as follows: RICHARD FLEMING WHO MADE THIS IN THE YEARE 1712; there is an upright flower stem between the 17 and the 12. This monument does not mark a burial and Richard Fleming is probably buried in Emlaghfad (SL033-14402-), with other members of that family, where there are five Fleming chest-tombs, three of which are very ornate (pers. comm. M. B. Timoney).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In low-lying level terrain, skirted by a stream, on the W side of Ballymote town. A late 13th-century Anglo-Norman fortress built by Richard de Burgh c. 1300 (Leask 1941, 69-70; Sweetman 1985-6; McNeill 1997, 101 and fig. 56; Sweetman 1999, 105-8). It appears to have been occupied for a short time before it was taken by the MacDonaghs in 1317 though probably not held permanently by them until after 1350 when the de Burgh influence started to wane. It is a large enclosure castle typical of the period and having close affinities with the castles built by Edward I in Wales.
The castle is almost square in plan (int. dims. 41.9m E-W; 40.1m N-S) and consists of a large twin-towered gateway, in the middle of the N wall, four angle towers and a tower midway along the E and W curtain walls (see plan Sweetman 1985-6, fig. 2). Similar castles of the same period are to be found at Ballintober and Roscommon town in county Roscommon, as well as at Ballyloughan, county Carlow (Brindley and Kilfeather 1993, Inv. no. 699). Another castle with close connections is the no longer extant Sligo Castle (O'Conor 2002).
The gatehouse is much ruined and has only its southern portion (back wall) standing to its full height. The northern section has been destroyed down to ground level. Partial excavation in 1981 revealed the full plan of the twin-towered gatehouse. The towers are three storeys high with a central gate passage which has the remains of a portcullis slot at its northern end. The chambers over the gate passage no longer exist nor do the upper chambers of the towers. Steps in the eastern tower give access to the first-floor level but there is now no evidence of how the upper floor was reached. There are the remains of a fireplace in each tower at ground-floor level. The first-floor level of the gatehouse, which has only its S wall standing, has mural passages and small chambers in it. The windows in the S wall central area, overlooking the passage, are smaller and out of line with those of the towers and are alterations. The outer curved walls of the towers had a double facing and were up to 3.2m thick. The towers are D-shaped (int. dims.: W tower 5.9m E-W; 3.3m N-S; E tower c. 6m N-S; 4.5m E-W). The gate passage is c. 9.5m long by 2.4m wide. The S face of the gatehouse has water spouts which would allow run-off into the enclosed area of the castle.
The NE angle tower is single storey, five-sided internally (5.5m SE-NW) and externally almost horseshoe-shaped. There are two opes with six steps up from ground level to each. The centre E wall tower is D-shaped with a solid or closed back or straight side and is 3 storeys high (int. ground floor 2.6m by 2.8m). The first floor is accessed from the battlement level only, the second floor via steps from the wall-walk level of the curtain wall. The first and second floors have fireplaces in the S wall. The ground floor appears to have been for storage only and can only be accessed at ground level. Along this section of the curtain wall, just below the wall-walk, is a large horizontal slot to take a wall-plate.
The much-ruined SE tower is also D-shaped with a closed back and is three storeys high. Internally it is five-sided with a stairs in the W wall, a chamber in the NE wall and with an arrow-loop. The garderobe at ground-floor level exits into a shallow ditch. The S curtain wall has a central doorway which leads to intramural steps at each side that lead to the wall-walk level. The total wall thickness here is 2.6m, the wall-walk is c. 1m wide. The SW tower is single storey and is open-backed. It is D-shaped externally and three-sided internally. It is very similar to the NE tower except that it has a garderobe, which exits into a drain outside the wall.
The central W curtain tower is three storeys high and is D-shaped with a closed back. Immediately inside the doorway at each side are intramural stairs. Those at the S lead directly to the parapets of the curtain wall but the other leads to the first and second floor chambers as well as the wall-walk. The wall-walk is one storey higher at this side than that of the E curtain. This was a residential tower with a garderobe at both ground- and first-floor levels. The NW tower is five-sided internally although two sides are very short. It appears now as a single storey tower but must have been originally two because of the height of the curtain wall adjoining it.
Excavations in 1981 (Sweetman 1985-6) showed that there was no moat on the S side of the castle but merely a flooded area. There is a slight base-batter on the towers and curtain walls which may be slightly greater if the low-lying flooded area continued around the castle originally. However there is no evidence at the gatehouse that there was ever a drawbridge and the garderobe exits are clearly visible as if they emptied into a shallow ditch or swamp.
The castle was repaired by Sir George Bingham c. 1580 when his 'arms' were erected on one of the towers (Ó Muraíle 2002, 241), but this plaque is now lost. The manuscript, known as the Book of Ballymote, is said to have been written, at least in part in Ballymote Castle c. 1391. It is now housed in the Royal Irish Academy, Dublin. The 'Red' Earl's Road (SL033-147----) was reputedly built by Richard de Burgh to link Ballymote Castle to Boyle Abbey, county Roscommon (RO006-068005-). According to Timoney and Timoney (2001, 21), de Burgh is also credited with building the road known as 'Bothar an Corrann' (SL033-145----) to get from his castle at Ballymote into county Roscommon. (Sweetman 1985-6, 114-24)

This is a national monument in State care (no. 638).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on the top of the S-facing slope of a drumlin. A raised circular area (26.5m N-S; 27m E-W) defined by two earthen banks and an intervening fosse. The inner bank (int. H 0.3m; ext. H 2.85m) is evident all round. There is a gentle slope (H 0.35m) from the base of the inner bank into the interior. There is a possible entrance at NW with a break (Wth 5m) in the inner bank, a slight causeway across the fosse and an opposing break (Wth 6.5m) in the outer bank. A second possible entrance occurs at ENE with a break (Wth 6m) in the inner bank, a slight causeway across the fosse and an opposing break (Wth 1.6m) in the outer bank. The intervening fosse (Wth at base 4m) is evident all round. The outer bank (int. H 0.8m; ext. H 0.3m) is evident S-N, with short sections also visible at NNE, E and SE. It is incorporated into a field boundary SE-S. There is a recent gap (Wth 4m) in the outer bank at SW. The interior is level, dry and clear of overgrowth.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on the top of a drumlin. A large steep-sided conical mound (diam. 21.5m; H 6m) denuded at E, exposing earth and stone. A slight depression (Wth 4m) visible at E may be the remains of a fosse. Lewis (1837, vol. 2, 189) mentioned under the parish of Kilmorgan 'several mounds of earth covering stone graves, in which bones and urns containing ashes have been found, whence it is inferred that a battle was anciently fought here' (SL033-211----). It is not known to which site or sites Lewis was referring but this bowl-barrow and the cairn (SL033-108----), also in Doomore townland, are both in the parish of Kilmorgan.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on level ground on top of a ridge. A roughly circular cairn (17m N-S; 16m E-W) of moss-covered limestone stones defined by a rocky scarp (ext. H 0.7m) all round apart from a short section at ENE where it is quarried away. The quarrying extends westwards into the interior for 14m to within 3m of the scarp at WSW and its base is on the old ground level beneath the cairn. Spoil from this quarrying has been dumped in a pile in the NW quadrant of the cairn. On the SE side of the quarry trench, near the scarp at E, is the remains of a stone-lined cist (SL033-108001-). Traces of kerbing and a shallow fosse (Wth 2.9m) were noted along SE arc during a previous inspection (pers. comm. M. Keane and J. Farrelly). Described by Wood-Martin (1887-8, 269) as '240 feet [73.15m] in circumference at base, 40 feet [12.19m] on the side, and at top there is a truncated cone about 12 feet [3.62m] in diameter. It is constructed of loose stones, with a covering of soil and grass'. By 1936 it was described as 'thirty feet [9.14m] high and one hundred and twenty feet [36.57m] in circumference' (MacDonagh 1936, 198).
Lewis (1837, vol. 2, 189) mentioned under the parish of Kilmorgan 'several mounds of earth covering stone graves, in which bones and urns containing ashes have been found, whence it is inferred that a battle was anciently fought here' (SL033-211----). It is not known to which site or sites Lewis was referring but this cairn and the bowl-barrow (SL033-104----) also in Doomore townland are both in the parish of Kilmorgan.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In the R.C. Church of the Immaculate Conception, Ballymote. A rectangular limestone block (L 0.49m; Wth 0.29m; H 0.15m) with a central circular slightly rounded hollow or bowl (diam. 0.22m; D 0.1m). This stoup has been at its present location within living memory and may have come from the nearby abbey (SL033-163001-) or from the former R. C. Church (now Loftus Hall) immediately E of the abbey. The former R. C. church was closed in 1864 and subsequently converted into the present parish hall. (pers. comm. M. A. Timoney, Feb 2004). There is also a font (SL033-115001-) in the church which was brought here in 1948 from Battlefield House (OS sheet 39) but whose original location is not known.

Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, Univesity College Cork.

raw_items.raw_text: Richard de Burgh, the Red Earl of Ulster, is credited with building this road

source_data.original_text:
Bóthar an Corann or Bothar na Slieve connected the town of Ballymote, Co. Sligo with Boyle, Co. Roscommon by a route around the SW side of Kesh Corran and to the W of the Bricklieve Mountains, a distance of c. 20km. According to Timoney and Timoney (2001, 21), Richard de Burgh, the Red Earl of Ulster, is credited with building this road to get from his castle at Ballymote (SL033-092----) into Roscommon. This entry deals only with that part of the road in Co. Sligo, i.e. from close to Ballymote as far as the Roscommon border. The road traverses a number of townlands over a number of the 1914 edition of the OS 6-inch sheets: OS 33: Ardsallagh/ Corhober/Mullaghcor; 
OS 39: Ardsallagh/Knocknacroy/Cross/Cloonagh/ Knocknawhishoge; 
OS 40:Carrowreagh/Dernaskeagh; OS 45: Meenmore/ Derrygolagh/Dernaskeagh. A possible link road between Bothar an Corann and Bothar an Iarla Ruaid (SL033-147---) goes from Greenan townland, around the S side of the Bricklieve Mountains, to Ballinafad.

Sections of Bóthar an Corann are recorded as five separate records (SL033-145---; SL039-031----; SL040-143----; SL040-153----; SL045-002----) commencing at Ballymote and following the route SE to the county boundary with Roscommon. Only sections of the road are indicated on these maps though it was, of course, continuous.

This section (SL033-145----) is located in undulating terrain of damp, rushy pasture and bog. Indicated on the 1914 OS 6-inch map as a stretch of road (L c. 2.7km NNW-SSE). The road is poorly preserved with some sections damaged or destroyed by land clearance and forestry. Other sections of it are still in use with various surfacing materials noted. The road from Keenaghan to Corhober is a public road (Wth 14-16m), surfaced with tarmac. The road undulates along this section and is defined on either side by earth and stone banks. The Red Earl's Road (SL033-147----) is, at its nearest point, c. 0.8km to the NE. The site of the medieval church (SL033-144001-) at Emlaghfad is c. 0.5km to the S. Beyond the junction accessing the R295 road (Ballymote-Boyle) in Corhober, the road is used as a private avenue to a house to the SE. The surface of the avenue is gravelled. From this house, the road skirts the NE side of a drumlin in Mullaghcor. Along this section the road (Wth 12m) is densely overgrown and is only in occasional use for herding cattle. The surface is rocky and in poor condition with the edges of the road defined by earth and stone banks. Beyond this the road is gravelled until it meets the main road (R295). The road crosses the R295 into the townland of Ardsallagh from where it extends in an ESE direction across undulating pasture, skirting the SW side of a low hill. This stretch of road (Wth 6.6m) (SL033-189----) is grass covered and scarped out of the hillslope and slightly raised on the downslope side (pers. comm. M. A. Timoney). It is not defined on either side here and appears sporadically as areas of harder ground and lighter patches of grass within pasture fields. The width of this section varies from 8m to 12m depending on ground conditions.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

Date of revision: 1 June 2011

source_data.original_text:
The Red Earl's Road, probably of medieval origin, linked the towns of Ballymote, Co. Sligo and Boyle, Co. Roscommon, by a route around the N and E sides of the Bricklieve Mountains (M. A. Timoney 1998, 155), a distance of c. 21km. It is said to have been built by Richard de Burgh, The Red Earl of Ulster, after the Norman conquest, to link his castle (SL033-092----) at Ballymote with Boyle Abbey (RO006-068005-), Co. Roscommon. The road traverses a number of townlands over a number of 6-inch sheets (OS 33: Bellanascarrow West/Roscrib East/Roscrib West/Ballinvoher; OS 34: Drumcormick/ Bricklieve/Tiraree; OS 40: Cloghoge Lower/Carrowkeel/Mullaghfarna/ Doonaveeragh/Knockroe/Cuilsheeghary More/Mountgaffeny/Ballinafad/Gortalough/ Ballaghboy/Cartron; OS 45: Ballaghboy/Cartron).

Sections of the road are recorded under five records (SL033-147----; SL034-159----; SL040-023----; SL040-197----; SL040-190----) commencing at Ballymote and following the route E and then S to the county boundary with Roscommon. Only sections of the road are indicated on the 1914 and 1941 OS 6-inch maps even though it was, of course, continuous. A possible link road between Bothar an Iarla Ruaid and Bothar an Corran (SL033-145----) goes from Greenan townland, around the S side of the Bricklieve Mountains, to Ballinafad. At its nearest point, Bothar an Corran is c. 0.8km to the SW. 

This section (SL033-147----) of the Red Earl's Road (L c. 2.5km) crosses undulating pasture with no obvious preference for ground conditions. Views vary along the route according to the terrain. It has been replaced by a modern tarred road (Wth 12-15m), bounded by earthen banks or stone walls, where it passes through the townlands of Bellanascarrow East and Roscrib West as far as the rath (SL033-125----) which is c. 20m to the N of the road in Roscrib East. To the E of this rath the road extends cross-country through Ballinvoher, following a large field boundary on its N side and is also visible in sections as a band of dark grass (Wth 6m). For the remainder of this section the road is beneath a disused lane (Wth 8-10m). According to local information, it continued to the W under a modern lane to meet the main road to the W of the Presbyterian Church at Graniamore.

source_data.original_text:
According to MacDonagh (1936, 197) this ruin is 'the remains of the fortified house' built by Jasper Brett; Brett was High Sheriff of Sligo in 1627-28 and 1635 (O'Dowd 1991, 58). Access to the ruined structure, which is known locally as a 'castle', was denied by the landowner but it was observed from the roadside. It consists of a SW gable wall (L 10.35m; T 0.25-0.45m) and returns of the NW (L 6.5m) and SE (L 3.1m) walls, of a two-storey house (wall measurements in Flynn 2003). The walls (H c. 5m) are of random mortared rubble with undressed corner quoins. Some red brick was also noted in the fabric of the walls, particularly at the broken ends of the NW and SE walls. No window embrasures survive. Joist-holes are visible on the inner face of the gable wall c. 2.5m above ground level. A lean-to shed stands against the external face of the gable wall. A series of low earthworks, evident immediately to the NE, E and S of the ruin, may be the remains of a bawn or structures associated with the house.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
Listed in the SMR (1989) and classified 'Enclosure(s)'. Not included in the RMP (1995). The original information came from aerial photograph (IASAP, 3043028-9). A field inspection in 1992 recorded that there were no features here except a quarry hole. (SMR file). It was revisited as the aerial photograph showed foundations of rectangular structures likely to be of 18th/19th century date. In undulating pasture, on gentle S-facing slope. The fragmentary remains of a rectangular house (19m NE-SW; 5m NW-SE) with earth and stone walls (int. H 0.2m; ext. H 0.25m). The walls survive on NE, SE and part of NW sides. The interior is level and clear of overgrowth. A return (L 2m) of the NW wall suggests a possible internal division, dividing the house into rooms of roughly equal size. A thickening of the SE wall (L 2.6m; T 1.55m) toward its SW end indicates the probable position of the fireplace. An earth and stone bank extends SE from E corner of this house linking it to another rectangular structure (12m NW-SE; 7m SW-NE) immediately to E. This structure, which may have been an outhouse, has earth and stone walls (int. H 0.35m; ext. H 0.4m) on all sides apart from NW where edge is defined by an inward facing scarp (H 0.75m). Breaks in the wall at the SW corner (Wth 1.8m) and at the SE end of NE wall (Wth 1.7m) may have been entrances. The interior is level with no evidence for internal division. The interior is flush with the external ground level on all sides except at NW where it is sunken. This is probably post-1700 AD in date.


Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC

source_data.original_text:
At the N edge of Ardrea Lough, a small inter-drumlin lake, and below an earlier shoreline. Land reclamation around the NE shore of the lake in the early 1990s had uncovered large quantities of archaeological material, including two quernstones, worked wood, broken flagstones and animal bones. As a result, a detailed survey of the lakeshore and an excavation of a possible crannog were undertaken by the Irish Archaeological Wetland Unit in 1992-3 (Moloney 1994, 70-71; Bermingham 1996, 31-3). The possible crannog was first identified as a number of layers of horizontal and longitudinally placed roundwoods overlaying a layer of flagstones; at the lake edge these layers were up to 0.5m deep (Bermingham 1996, 31). These layers were subsequently destroyed due to further reclamation and excavation revealed that underneath them was a layer of gravel in which was a series of posts (max. diam. 0.16m; max. L 1.27m) which may have formed part of an enclosing feature or have functioned as piles over which the stone flag surface had been laid (ibid., 32). Present remains consist of a rectangular area (10m N-S; 26m E-W) in which pieces of worked timbers, animal bones and scattered stones are visible as well as roundwood, brushwood and shells. According to local information, there was a low mound here which was levelled long before the excavation took place. Two fulachtaí fia (SL033-195001-; SL033-195002-) are in the immediate vicinity.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on the NE-facing shoulder of a drumlin. This barrow was partially excavated by Keane and Farrelly (1993, 56; 1994, 71) in 1992 and 1993. It was described prior to excavation as a concave circular area (int. diam. 9m) raised slightly above the external ground level and enclosed by an earth and stone bank (Wth 1.4m; ext. H 0.6m); a gap (Wth 4m) was noted in the bank at E; faint traces of an external fosse were visible along the N arc; the interior sloped gently to E and the bank height diminished towards E (Keane and Farrelly 1993, 56). Excavation revealed that the bank and fosse continue all round and that the possible entrance at E was a worn down section of bank (Keane and Farrelly 1994, 71). An oblong pit (1.5m x 0.8m), containing a dump of stones in a charcoal-rich sandy clay was uncovered in the NE quadrant. A large modern pit (3.4m N-S; 3.8m E-W) was also excavated in the interior which truncated all the internal layers in the other cuttings (ibid.). No evidence for house structures was found which suggests that this was not a habitation site and this is supported by the continuous bank and fosse (ibid.). Finds included quantities of worked chert and a flint thumb scraper (ibid.). A radiocarbon date obtained from charcoal from the base of the bank places the construction of this barrow in the Iron Age (Farrelly and Keane 2002, 100). There is a mound barrow (SL039-010----) in the adjoining field c. 190m to S and a ring-barrow (SL039-011----) c. 230m to SE. source_data.original_text:
In pasture, at the base of a gradual NW-facing slope. A spring well appears to be located within an area (c. 3m NW-SE; c. 4m NE-SW) of grass-covered waterlogged ground bordered to SW by a low bedrock facade (L c. 2m; H 1m). There is no evidence of recent veneration at this well. In 1942-4 it was recorded that no pilgrimages had been made to it in the memory of the oldest inhabitants (ITA). In 1836 it was recorded that the well was known as 'Tobar na Naomh by the inhabitants of the surrounding townland' but in Abbeyville it was known as 'St. Bridget's well or Tobar Naomh Bríghde' (OSL, 148). It was also noted in 1836 that while there were no 'stations' then held at the well, they had been held there at one time (OSNB vol. 1, 351).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
Bóthar an Corann or Bothar na Slieve connected the town of Ballymote, Co. Sligo with Boyle, Co. Roscommon by a route around the SW side of Kesh Corran and to the W of the Bricklieve Mountains, a distance of c. 20km. According to Timoney and Timoney (2001, 21), Richard de Burgh, the Red Earl of Ulster, is credited with building this road to get from his castle at Ballymote (SL033-092----) into Roscommon. This entry deals only with that part of the road in Co. Sligo, i.e. from close to Ballymote as far as the Roscommon border. The road traverses a number of townlands over a number of the 1914 edition of the OS 6-inch sheets: OS 33: Ardsallagh/ Corhober/Mullaghcor; 
OS 39: Ardsallagh/Knocknacroy/Cross/Cloonagh/ Knocknawhishoge; 
OS 40:Carrowreagh/Dernaskeagh; OS 45: Meenmore/ Derrygolagh/Dernaskeagh. A possible link road between Bothar an Corann and Bothar an Iarla Ruaid (SL033-147---) goes from Greenan townland, around the S side of the Bricklieve Mountains, to Ballinafad.

Sections of Bóthar an Corann are recorded as five separate records (SL033-145---; SL039-031----; SL040-143----; SL040-153----; SL045-002----) commencing at Ballymote and following the route SE to the county boundary with Roscommon. Only sections of the road are indicated on these maps though it was, of course, continuous.

This section (SL039-31----) is a relatively long portion (L c. 2.3km). It is mainly orientated NW-SE, is tarred and is in use as a byroad. It is 3-4m wide and is flanked by walls, which in parts have been replaced by post-and-wire fencing. A section (L 0.8km) of the road that extends from Knocknacroy into Knocknawhishoge is not tarred and survives as a grassed-over metalled track flanked by field fences and currently used as a farm trackway.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

Date of revision: 1 June 2011

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, in the NE corner of a field at the base of a W-facing slope. The well has been infilled and its location is marked only by an area of uneven ground covered by a clump of irises. This corner of the field is neglected and covered by long grass. No enclosing structure could be discerned. On a previous site inspection in 1994 the well was described as enclosed by rectangular stone setting (1.2m N-S; 0.8m E-W) (SMR (1989) file). According to local information, the well was probably covered over during field-clearance activity in recent years. A few people in the locality know of this holy well though in 1942-4 it was recorded that no pilgrimages had been made to it in the memory of the oldest resident (ITA). In 1836 it was recorded as 'Tobar Bearaigh (Barry) surrounded by a turret of stone work (as the inhabitants call it) which is now greatly injured' (OSL, 147). It was also recorded that the well was closed and that only a little water was then running from it (ibid.).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

The natural slope immediately to S of the rath has been extensively quarried out.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on top of a drumlin. The rath was described in 1985 (SMR (1989) file) as a roughly pear-shaped area (19m N-S; 33m E-W), tapering towards the E, defined N-SW by a low earthen bank and SW-N by a more substantial bank (Wth 1.25m; int. H 0.3m; ext. H 1m) topped with a hedge and a post and wire fence and covered with overgrowth. A shallow external fosse-like depression was evident SE-SW and a shallow drain was evident outside the bank SW-N. The E portion of the interior was raised to compensate for the hillslope but the interior retained a gentle slope down to E. A scatter of stone was noted inside the S perimeter in an area overgrown with bushes. The bank was quarried into at NNE. The perimeter appeared to turn inwards along the S side, suggesting that the rath was once circular with a subtriangular area added to E side. It is indicated as an embanked circular area on the 1838 OS 6-inch map. On subsequent inspection in 1994 the remains consisted of a raised area (int. diam. 29.5m N-S; 11.2m E-W), enclosed by an earthen bank (Wth 3m; int. H 1.2m; ext. H 1.5m), the interior of which was uneven and sloped down to N. No remains of the fosse was visible.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In pasture, on a level strip of ground on the NE bank of a stream. Indicated as an embanked circular enclosure on the 1838 OS 6-inch map on the E bank of a stream. The course of the stream was altered on the 1914 OS 6-inch map and indicated as forming the straight side of a D-shaped raised area with a mound at the centre. The enclosure has been levelled and a slightly raised D-shaped area (c. 34m NW-SE; c. 28m NE-SW) is evident, defined by a slight rise NNW-SSE with an infilled external fosse (Wth 1.5-2m) E-SSE. The stream (recut to serve as a drain) forms the straight side at SW. The interior is slightly domed, sloping down from the centre to the perimeter where it merges with the surrounding field. The interior surface is poached by cattle, uneven and covered with rough grass. There is an oval quarry pit (6m NW-SE; 4.6m NE-SW; D 0.95m) S of centre. A few metres SW of the pit is an electricity pylon. A shallow pit dug on the edge of the stream has slightly truncated the NNW edge of the enclosure.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In a wet meadow on the SW edge of Feenagh Lough. A circular low-mound crannog (22m N-S; 22m E-W; H 1.37m above the ground). A mid-mound (4.2m N-S; 4.5m E-W) is located off-centre to W and surrounded by a plateau (7.3m N-S; 3m E-W) that is most distinct to the N and S. The plateau is surrounded by a berm (c. 12m wide along the E arc, narrowing to 2.5m at W), that drops off to a distinct edge. This crannog was excavated by A. Mahr in the 1920s (NMI) but the results of the excavation were never published. On the berm at NE is a hollow (diam. c. 6m) possibly resulting from the excavation. The crannog is overgrown with grass which contrasts in colour with that of the surroundings. At least three dug-out canoes have been found along the S side of the lake (pers. comm. M. A. Timoney).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In level damp pasture, at the base of a gradual E-facing slope. A trapezoidal platform (27.7m at N, 23.4m at E, 24m at S, 18.5m at W) defined on the W and N sides by an earthen bank (Wth c. 3.5m; int. H 0.55m; ext. H 1.6m at N) and on the E and S sides by a scarp (H 1.3m). The flat-bottomed fosse (Wth 3.4m) is evident outside the bank on the N side while on the W side it is evident only as a shallow depression (Wth c. 3m). An external bank (Wth c. 3m; int. H 1.4m; ext. H 0.3m) is evident on the N side. A road skirts the scarp on the E side at a distance of 1.5m. On the S side the scarp drops to a low irregular terrace (Wth 3-4.5m; H 0.3m). A strip of flat damp ground separates the terrace from a road. The interior is level and grassy. Hawthorn and ash trees and dense clumps of brambles mark the perimeter.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
On the N end of a gravel ridge with restricted views to N and E and more extensive views to S and W. Described in 1995 (pers. comm. M. Keane and J. Farrelly) as a barrow (original overall diam. 11m WNW-ESE), the S half of which is destroyed by quarrying and the E edge of which is truncated by a field boundary. The remains consist of an arc of bank (Wth 4.2m; ext. H 0.55m) W-E. The section of the interior visible in the quarry face showed that the barrow was composed of gravel and large stones covered by a layer of topsoil. A small V-shaped pit (diam. 0.25m; D 0.3m), filled with dark brown clay, was also visible in the exposed section. (Farrelly and Keane 2002, 98)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

This is the present location of one (SL044-003006-) of four cross-slabs found in Knockmore graveyard (SL044-003003-) in the late 1970s and early 1980s. source_data.original_text:
In pasture, located on terrace on the S-facing slope of a ridge. The location provides extensive views in a broad sweep from ESE–NW; in the immediate foreground at S–SW, the slope drops into a valley backed by an arc of hills. Views are blocked N–NE where the slope rises to the summit of the ridge. 
This enclosure is not indicated on the 1838 and 1914 OS 6-inch maps. It has been levelled in the relatively distant past, but is evident in current aerial views and at ground level as a circular area (diam. c. 20-21m) outlined by low undulations.
At ground level the enclosure is most clearly defined at SSE–SW, where a broad, low curving scarp (ext. H 1.2m at S) is cut into the hill slope, coinciding with the contour of the natural terrace, and at NW where there is a low rise or undulation, representing an arc of levelled bank. At N–E the barely discernible outline of a levelled field boundary skirts the enclosure, respecting its curve and continuing in a straight line to N and S beyond the enclosure: this is evident at N-NNE as curving inward-facing scarp (H 0.8m), which diminishes and peters out towards the E. A slight depression/gap (Wth 2-2.5m) intervenes between the enclosure and this skirting field boundary suggesting that the enclosure may have an enclosing fosse. An extant N–S field fence truncates the W edge of the enclosure, and a short length of a roughly E-W field bank skirts the SW arc. The interior of the enclosure is relatively level in the N half, with a slight slope down in the S half, mirroring the natural terrace.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on the level top of a low hill/drumlin at a bend in the Owenmore River which loops around the E side of the hill. There are good views along the river valley, and over the surrounding undulating landscape. It is overlooked by a higher hill c. 400m to W.
This rath is not shown on any edition of the OS 6-inch map, but is visible in aerial imagery.
A grass-covered circular platform (31.6m N−S; 34m E−W) defined by a scarp (H 0.5-0.6m at N & S, 0.75m at E). The scarp is low for most of the circuit, with a gradual break of slope between the top and sides, suggesting that it has been partly levelled out in the past. It is more substantial on the E arc where it is enhanced by a gentle natural fall of ground. At W the scarp is slighted by a later N-S field bank/hedgerow. A band of damp ground (Wth c. 4m) immediately outside the scarp on the S arc possibly indicates a fosse but it cannot be traced elsewhere. 
The rath is crossed centrally on an E−W axis by a field bank (Wth 2m) with parallel field ditch (now silted up) (Wth 1.4m; D 0.2-0.3m). A few hawthorn trees grow along the line of the field bank.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a slight E-facing slope on top of a ridge. A raised circular area (33m N-S; 32m E-W) defined by an inner earth and stone bank, an intervening fosse and an outer earthen bank. The inner earthen bank (int. H 0.7m; Ext. H 1.95m) encloses the interior WSW-ENE and SE-SSW. The inner bank has been quarried away SSW-WSW and eroded by cattle breaks at NW (Wth 6m), at N (Wth 4m) and at S (Wth 4m). The break at S has a slight causeway across the fosse caused by outward slumping of the inner bank. There is a possible entrance at E (Wth 7m) with an adjacent area to S disturbed by quarrying. The intervening fosse (Wth 3m at base) and the outer earthen bank (int. H 0.85m; ext. H. 0.55m) are evident SE-NE. A field boundary truncates the outer bank NE-SE, a second field boundary abuts the external face of the outer bank along the W arc. The interior is undulating and strewn with rocks and slopes gently down to E. Some of the undulations may be the result of quarrying. A small rectangular earthwork is located just outside the outer bank at NNE. This earthwork consists of a raised rectangular area (4m N-S; 4.7m E-W) defined by an earth and stone bank (int. H 0.3m; ext. H 0.45m). The interior is slightly concave in profile and clear of overgrowth. On the SE side of this earthwork, outside the base of the bank at the SE corner, a shallow drain (D 0.3m) with an earthen bank (H 0.45m) on its N side (both orientated E-W) has been dug extending E to a field boundary. Roughly 1.5m to the W of the rectangular earthwork is a series of low earth and stone mounds (diam. 1.5-2.5m; H 0.8-1m). A low earthen bank (ext. H 0.25m) which runs parallel to the W edge of the rectangular earthwork defines the limit of these mounds on the E side.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In undulating rocky pasture, on a slight SE-facing slope. Immediately to E of two house sites (SL033-060002-; SL033-060004-) and another relict field (SL033-060003-). A pentagonal field (20m N-S; 22m E-W) defined by an earth and stone bank (int. H 0.35m; ext. H 0.45m) with an external fosse (D 0.4m) or drain on the NE, SE, SW and NW sides. The N side is defined by a WSW-ENE relict field bank (int. H 0.65m) with a relict drain (D 0.7m) on its N side. The interior slopes gently down to S and is gently undulating. The natural ground level immediately to N of the field is higher than that of the interior. A short stretch of a relict field bank abuts the field at S. The banks enclosing this area are exactly similar in form to the relict field banks visible across the area. This enclosure appears to be a small relict field being part of the more extensive field system. Similar small relict fields are visible on the ground and the RMP (1995) map to the E and SE of this site. This is part of a larger field system (SL033-070----).

Another relict linear field boundary (Wth 2.6m; H c. 0.4m; L c. 300m) on a NNW-SSE axis, with a fosse (D 0.2m) on its E side, cuts through the circular enclosure (SL033-077001-) and two of the raths (SL033-076----; SL033-077002-).

source_data.original_text:
In gently undulating pasture. A roughly circular area (98m N-S; 99m E-W) defined by two earthen banks and an intervening fosse. The inner bank (int. H 0.5m; ext. H 1m) is evident W-NNW while elsewhere the interior is defined by a scarp. There is a possible entrance (Wth 16m) at WNW with breaches in both banks and slight infilling of the fosse. The fosse is evident all round and has a broad U-shaped profile (Wth 4.5m at base). The outer bank (int. H 0.75m; ext. H 0.3m) is evident SE-NE with a further short stretch at ESE. It is broken by gaps at NW (Wth 12m) and NNW (Wth 6m) and has been incorporated into a field boundary NE-ESE. The interior undulates gently and slopes gently from the centre toward the enclosing elements. A relict field boundary (see SL033-075001-) with a fosse on its E side crosses the interior on a NNW-SSE axis. There is a rath (SL033-077001-) and souterrain (SL033-077003-) in the SE quadrant, abutting the inner edge of the fosse at SSE. Another rath (SL033-076----) is 14m to NNW and a third (SL033-078----) c. 100m to SE. A field system (SL033-075001-) lies immediately to E.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
At Emlaghnaghtan rath (SL033-083----). In the S half is a circular earthwork surrounded by a stone wall; on top of the enclosing bank on the S side of the earthwork is a stone memorial with a plaque bearing a coat of arms and inscribed 'RICHARD FLEMING WHO MADE THIS IN THE YEARE 1712'; there is an upright flower stem between the 17 and the 12. According to local tradition, this monument does not mark a burial and Richard Fleming is probably buried in Emlaghfad (SL033-144002-) with other members of that family (Flynn 2003-4, 22-3).

source_data.original_text:
On top of a ridge, in undulating pasture. A circular conical mound (H c. 6m) with a flat top (diam. 29m), enclosed by a fosse (Wth 8m) with an external earthen bank (Wth 3.5m; int. H 1.8m; ext. H 2m). The entrance (Wth 3.5m) is at S where there is a ramp up to the side of the mound. There is an oval hollow (L c. 5m) in the E half of the top of the mound. Knox (1911, 222-3) considered the site had 'the appearance of a high Norman mote', and it is listed as a motte by Glasscock (1975, 109). This may be the site of the castle of Ath-na-Gail, erected in 1265 by MacWilliam Burke and demolished in 1270 by Aedh O Connor (Graham 1988, 121).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

font was brought to the church in Ballymote in 1948

source_data.original_text:
This was listed in the SMR (1989) as 'Font (original location)' under the number SL039-132004-. This monument is located in the R. C. Church in Ballymote and was believed locally to have come from Battlefield church and graveyard (SL039-132001 and SL039-132002-). However, in Feb. 2004 Martin Timoney informed the Archaeological Survey unit, UCC, that the font was brought to the church in Ballymote in 1948 by James. P. McGarry from Battlefield House and not from Battlefield church. Its original location is not known and it has been assigned a record number (SL033-115001-) at its present location in Ballymote. 

The font is a sub-cubical sandstone block (L 0.35m; Wth 0.3m; H 0.28m) into which a round-bottomed sub-cylindrical bowl (diam. 0.2m; D 0.19m) has been cut, leaving walls 0.04m thick. In section the block is subcircular at the top, octagonal midway down and square at the base. There are bulbous projections at the bottom of the four smaller chamfered faces. The broken off section at the top has been repaired with cement. It was at one time stored on the lawn in fornt of the church at Ballymote but was moved inside into the boiler house.

Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, University College Cork.

Date of upload: 15 May 2009

On a steep E-facing slope, in an area of unused ground between a drystone field boundary and a recently erected farm building (5m to S). A rectangular gable-ended structure (4.2m NE-SW; 3.95m NW-SE; wall T 0.7m) built of uncoursed limestone rubble in lime mortar. A ground-floor doorway, at the SE end of the NE wall, gives access to a barrel-vaulted chamber without windows. There is a small lintelled ope in the SE wall at first-floor level; access to this area was not gained but at least four tiers of nesting-boxes are visible. Projecting from the centre of the NW wall is a flat stone directly above which is a small opening in the wall; this must have been the entry point for pigeons accessing the loft. This structure is presumably associated with Ballynaglogh church (SL033-140001-) 40m to the ENE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

raw_items.raw_text: By the 1830s a new C of I parish church for Emlaghfad had been built

source_data.original_text:
On the flat summit of a hill, within a possible ecclesiastical enclosure and in the centre of Emlaghfad graveyard (SL033-144002-). The roofless ruin of a rectangular church (int. dims. 21.3m E-W; 6.2m N-S) with a square 3-storey tower (int. L 3.8m) at its W end. Though the style of the windows and doorways throughout the structure is uniformly 18th century and dates to the use of the building as a C of I parish church (SL033-144006-), the side-walls are noticeably thinner (by c. 0.2m) at its W end (L c. 6m). This suggests that the core of the E end may be that of the medieval parish church though no architectural features of that period are evident. The church is entered through a doorway in the W wall of the tower. This has a limestone door-surround with block-and-start jambs and a prominent keystone. The ground and second floors of the tower and the body of the church are lit by windows with surrounds in the style of the entrance doorway (all are blocked up). The first floor of the tower has oculus windows. The W end of the church interior is overgrown with elder trees and a mature evergreen tree fills its E end. The latter area contains a number of 19th-century headstones and one rectangular slab, lying on the ground, with a date of 1709. Floor timbers are missing from the tower, whose external walls are covered with ivy. There are pyramid pinnacles on the top of its corners. By the 1830s a new C of I parish church for Emlaghfad had been built in Ballymote (McTernan 1995; 1997; M. B. Timoney 1996), 1.2km to the NNW. A stretch of the road known as Bothar an Corann (SL033-145----) is c. 0.5km to the N.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
Within a possible ecclesiastical enclosure (SL034-144005-). A trapezoidal graveyard (c. 50m E-W; c. 60m N-S at W end; c. 40m N-S at E end) enclosed by a stone wall. The entrance, with plain stone pillars and a wrought iron gate, is at the W end of the S wall and there is a similar entrance at the W end of the N wall. At the centre is the ruin of the C of I parish church of Emlaghfad which probably incorporates the core of the medieval parish church (SL033-144001-). An area immediately S of the church contains a collection of 18th- and 19th-century chest-tombs and elaborate headstones belonging to a number of prominent Protestant families from the area (McTernan 1995; 1997). The earliest headstone noted was dated 1709 and lies within the church. A bullaun stone (SL033-144007-) was recently found within the interior of the graveyard. To the E, S and W are the remains of a bastioned fort (SL033-144008-).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In Emlaghfad graveyard (SL033-144002-). A C of I church built on or near the site of the medieval parish church of Emlaghfad and the site of a monastery founded by St Colmcille (Gwynn and Hadcock 1970, 383). This is a rectangular church (int.: 21.3m E-W; 6.2m N-S) with a square three-storey tower (int. L 3.8m) at its W end. It is entered through a doorway in the W wall of the tower. This has a limestone door-surround with block-and-start jambs and a prominent keystone. The ground and second floors of the tower and the body of the church are lit by windows with surrounds in the style of the entrance door (all are now blocked up). The first floor of the tower has occulus windows. The W end of the church interior is overgrown with elder trees and a mature tree shelters its E end. The latter area contains a number of 19th-century headstones and one rectangular slab, lying on the ground, with a date of 1709. Floor timbers are missing from the tower; the exterior walls are covered with ivy and there are pyramid pinnacles on the top corners. The style of the church is mid-18th-century; it was replaced in 1818 by a new church in Ballymote (Lewis 1837, vol. 1, 599) 1.2km to NNW. A stretch of the road known as Bothar an Corann (SL033-145----) is c. 0.5km to the N. This is post-1700 AD in date.


Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC

Date of upload: 04 January 2012

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on the summit of a drumlin with excellent views in all directions. A roughly circular area (51m N-S; 53m E-W) defined by the remains of two earthen banks and an intervening fosse. The inner bank (int. H 0.25m; ext. H 0.7m) is evident SE-NNW; elsewhere the interior is defined by a scarp. Two gaps noted in the inner bank at SSE and SW, with slight causeways (Wth 4m and 6m respectively) across the fosse, may be the result of livestock damage. The fosse is most clearly evident NNW-SW and only barely discernible elsewhere. The outer bank (int. H 0.6m; ext. H 0.3m) survives NNW-SE with faint traces of it visible SE-SSE and two further short sections at S and SSW. The interior undulates very gently and is dry and clear of overgrowth. There is a bowl-barrow (SL033-149002-) in the SW quadrant. A relict earth and stone field boundary joins the inner bank at WNW and another joins the outer edge of the fosse at SW. Similar field boundaries join the outer bank at NNW, NNE and SE. The section of the outer bank between the two boundaries NNW-SE seems to have been augmented in height and width to act as a field boundary. Included in a list of hillforts and hilltop enclosures by Condit, Gibbons and Timoney (1991, 62).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
On the W side of Ballymote town; in the NE corner of Ballymote graveyard (SL033-163002-). The remains of this friary consist of a rectangular gable-ended church (int. 28.5m E-W; 6.7m N-S; wall T c. 1.05m), built of roughly coursed limestone in a lime mortar. The N and E walls stand to near full height but the S and W walls are reduced a little in height. The structure was repaired in the 20th century by the OPW.
The central doorway in the W wall is missing its door surround. Directly overhead, externally, is a limestone head with a three-tiered crown/tiara surmounted by a cross; H. G. Leask in an unpublished report dated 1940 (SMR (1989) file) noted that this might be the representation of a pope (but see Conlan 1991, 5). There is a smaller doorway near the E end of the N wall, which is rebuilt. Inside it, on the E side, is a broken limestone stoup, on the undersurface of which is a damaged carving of a beast, possibly an amphisbaena (pers. comm. M. A. Timoney). The E gable contains a large central window. The internal edge of the embrasure is plain except for a soffit rib with chamfered edges. Only a single jambstone and bottom corner stone, both on the N side, survive of the window tracery. Near the W end of the S wall is a tall wide, open archway (Wth 3.5m). A drawing dating from 1779 (Harbison 2002, fig. 67) shows a gabled structure against the S wall in this area but nothing of it stands. In the same illustration, a second gabled projection is shown further E on the S wall (ibid.). This is reduced to a pile of rubble (c. 5.9m N-S; c. 3.8m E-W). There are also three window opes in the S wall. The interior of the church contains many 18th- and 19th-century burials. A limestone stoup (SL033-115----) (H 0.15m; 0.49m x 0.29m) with a central round flat-bottomed bowl (diam. 0.22m; D 0.1m), which is in the nearby RC Church in Ballymote, may have come from the friary or from the former RC Church (now Loftus Hall) immediately E of the friary (pers. comm. M. A. Timoney). 
These are the remains of a Franciscan Third Order Regular foundation (Ó Muraíle 2002, 241, n. 35), which was given a papal licence in 1444 , was attacked and burned c. 1483 and by 1584 was 'totally ruined' (Gwynn and Hadcock 1970, 268). According to Conlan (1988, 108), it was 'taken over by the First Order c. 1643, and was used by them for nearly a hundred years afterwards.'

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

A drain truncates the E side of a horseshoe-shaped grass-covered mound (15.4m N-S; 10.2m E-W to edge of drain; H 0.35m). An opening (Wth 2m) faces SW toward the lake. There is a possible fulacht fia (SL033-195002-) immediately to SE and a possible crannog (SL033-194----) in the immediate vicinity. (Bermingham 1996, 31)

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on top of an elongated flat-topped knoll with high steep rocky sides, giving excellent views in all directions. A subrectangular area (57m NE-SW; 25.7m NW-SE) defined on the SE side by a steep linear scarp (H 1m) with exposed limestone bedrock, on top of a less steep slope (H c. 6-7m). The SW side (H c. 2.5m), also broken by rock outcrops, is defined by a steep but lower scarp with an external fosse (Wth 7m; ext. D 1m). Skirting the fosse is a stony bank (Wth 1.2m), possibly a field boundary, that extends to NNE. The NW side is defined by a scarp (H c. 7-8m) which appears even higher and steeper than the SE side and in plan projects outward slightly in a shallow convex curve. The NE side comprises a straight scarp (H 2-2.5m) incorporating, slightly SE of centre, an entrance in the form of a slumped ramp-like gap (Wth 2m). A narrow stony bank (Wth 1.6m; H 0.65m) extends across the SW end of the interior c. 2m in from the edge of the scarp. A large, roughly D-shaped raised area (c. 28m NW-SE; c.18m NE-SW) abuts the NW side of the interior and is defined at NW by the edge of the enclosure and elsewhere by a curving scarp (H c. 1m). Immediately to SW is a possible hut site (SL039-058002-). The floodplain of the Owenmore River is to the E.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

A roughly circular area (c. 31m N-S; c. 34m E-W) crossed E of centre by the remains of a N-S trackway evident as a depression (Wth 3.2m; D 0.35m) bordered on its E side by a wall. To W of the wall the rath is evident as a slightly raised semicircular area (c. 31m N-S; 21m E-W to field wall) defined by a scarp (H 1.3m) S-N and covered with mature coniferous trees. To E of the wall the rath has been levelled to a flat area c. 0.5-0.7m lower than the W half. A large galvanised iron shed obliterates the NE quadrant but a slight curving undulation ESE-S appears to preserve the original outline of the rath. There is a souterrain (SL039-091002-) close to the scarp at W.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on the flat summit of a hill with excellent views of the surrounding countryside. An earthen platform (73m N-S; 90m E-W) defined by a scarp (max. H 0.65-0.8m), eroded in places and with a low internal lip (Wth 1.6-1.8m; H 0.2m), is evident outside the E, S and W sides of the graveyard (SL033-144002-) at Emlaghfad. The expanded and slightly rounded corners of this platform project 15-18m beyond the corners of the graveyard. Midway along each of its three sides, the platform is indented to within 8-9m of the graveyard wall. A N-S road, immediately outside the W wall of the graveyard, cuts through the W side of the platform, bordering the NW projecting corner as well as truncating the SW projecting corner. The SE corner remains intact while the NE corner is incorporated into a field boundary. A disused 19th-century house overlies the W end of the S side of the earthwork. There are no visible remains of the earthwork on the N side of the graveyard. Many mature trees and bushes grow on the platform. While the function of this earthwork remains uncertain, its star-shaped ground plan is suggestive of a bastioned fort.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In the corner of a field, on a N-facing slope. A waterlogged muddy overgrown area and some moss-covered stones mark the site of the well. A local legend, recorded in 1836, told that the mother of Cormac Mac Airt gave birth to Cormac while collecting water at Tober Cormac but while she was asleep the baby was taken by a wolf to a cave at Kesh (SL039-034----) to SE; some years later Cormac was returned to his mother (OSL, 161). A stretch of the road known as Bothar an Corann (SL033-145----) is c. 80m to the SW. (Kielty 2001, 4)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In a grassy clearing in a coniferous plantation, on the gentle SSE-facing slope of Kesh Corann. A slightly raised subcircular area (c. 21m N-S; 18m E-W) defined NE-SE by slight rise and SE-SW by a broadly slumped scarp (H 0.7m). Elsewhere the enclosing element is less obvious and at N it appears to be truncated by a forestry trench. The interior slopes gently down to S and is covered in rough grass and bisected by several E-W forestry drills. Trees are planted right up to the edge of the enclosure. An external fosse (Wth 2.3m; D 0.3m), noted along the E arc in 1993 (SMR (1989) file), is no longer evident. There is a barrow (SL040-003001-) and a circular enclosure (SL040-003002-) c. 40m to N. A hut site (SL040-005----) lies c. 50m to W.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
(In the Carrowkeel-Kesh Corann passage tomb cemetery). On the summit of Kesh Corann with a magnificent outlook in all directions. Within and close to the N edge of a hilltop enclosure (SL040-009---). This is a circular cairn (diam. 26m; H c. 4-5m) at the top of which there is a small pile of stones, apparently a 19th-century OS trigonometrical station. A hole (4m x 3m; D 0.5m) has been dug into the E slope of the cairn and there is a larger hole extending from the summit downslope to the ENE. The cairn stands on what appears to be a prepared platform (diam. c. 35m), the perimeter of which is almost 5m beyond the base of the cairn. The platform is now substantially grass-grown and in places, especially at the N, peat-grown. It is c. 0.8m high around the greater part of the perimeter but reaches 2m high at the N over falling ground. Kerbstones are intermittently visible along or just inside the platform perimeter, in particular on the southern side. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 84)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).
