source_data.original_text:
In heather-covered blanket bog at the N end of a level plateau on top of Kesh Corann. A large pear-shaped area (c. 170m N-S; c. 170m E-W) defined by a low stony wall (Wth 2.5m; H 0.4m) engulfed in blanket bog. The wall can be traced as a slight rise SW-SE and short sections of it are exposed at NW revealing a jumble of stones and slabs. The wall coincides with a natural break of slope NNW-E, marking the N edge of the plateau. At N, it tops a vertical scarp of exposed bedrock (H 1.7m). The wall is difficult to trace SE-SW and it appears that portions of it may be covered in bog. A possible passage tomb (SL040-008----) lies within and close to the N end of this hilltop enclosure. Condit, Gibbons and Timoney (1991, 62) noted that while this enclosure follows the contour of the limestone terrace on the hill it 'does not seem to exploit the natural defenses of the hill'.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

Not included in the SMR (1989) but listed in the RMP (1995) and classified 'House'. Not shown on any edition of the OS 6-inch map. In upland boggy and rocky pasture, at the base of the NE-facing slope of Kesh Corann. The remains of a rectangular two-roomed structure (long-axis N-S) with sod-covered stone walls (T 2.1m; int. H 1m; ext. H 0.7m). Both the southern room (7.9m N-S; 3.2m E-W) and the northern room (3.05m N-S; 3.1m E-W) are filled with collapsed stones. A garden area (7.8m x 7m) to S is enclosed by an earthen bank (int. H 0.3m; ext. H 0.5m). An enclosure (SL040-003----) is c. 50m to E. This is likely to be post-1700 AD in date.

source_data.original_text:
Located on the W bank of a stream, in a shallow, boggy, rush-grown valley at the foot of the NE side of Kesh Corann. A passage tomb (SL040-006001-) crowns the top of a steep-sided hill which rises immediately to W of the stream. There is a rath (SL040-007----) 100m to SE on the low ridge that borders the E side of the stream. 
A layer of burnt stone in dark soil with charcoal inclusions is exposed in section immediately beneath the sod line in the W bank of the N-flowing stream. The nature and extent of the layer is uncertain as it is visible only along a short section (L 1m) of the stream edge which has been eroded by cattle. A slight rise in ground level (L 2-3m N-S; Wth 1-1.5m) is evident in a narrow strip parallel to the stream, but it is not possible to trace the original limits/outline of the possible burnt mound. A small deposit of burnt stone is also exposed in the E bank of the stream. 

Compiled by: Jane O’Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 26 November 2019

source_data.original_text:
In rough pasture, at the top of an E-facing slope, in the NE corner of Kilmorgan graveyard (SL034-081002-). This church is indicated as a rectangular structure (c. 20m E-W) on the 1838 OS 6-inch map. The E gable (ext. 7.24m N-S; T 1m) with returns of the S (ext. 7.7m) and N (ext. 12m) walls, constructed of random-rubble mortared limestone, survive. There is no trace of the W end. The E gable has a central window embrasure with a single round-headed light (Wth 0.25m; H 1.8m) which is chamfered and rebated externally. Near the E end of the S wall is another window embrasure, with a double light which is missing the upper part of its mullion and the central part of the top. This unusual light was formed from a single block of limestone, including the mullion. There is a wall-press under the E side of this window, on the internal wall-face. The N wall is missing a central portion (L c. 3m) which has been roughly repaired as this forms part of the boundary wall of the graveyard. There is a substantial crack at the SE corner. The interior contains 19th-century headstones and low uninscribed grave-markers. 
These are the remains of the medieval parish church of Kilmorgan (Timoney and Timoney 2000). A field system (SL034-081003-) lies to the W and a holy well (SL034-081006-) lies c. 200m to the N. The site of a mill (SL034-081005-) lies c. 50m to the N.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
A rectangular graveyard (c. 38m SE-NW; 22m NE-SW) enclosed by a stone wall. Access is through a piered entrance in the W wall; these may be the 'pair of pillars' erected here in 1820 (Timoney and Timoney 2000). The ruin of the medieval parish church of Kilmorgan (SL034-081001-) occupies the NE corner. Headstones date from the 18th to the 20th centuries and there are also a number of collapsed chest-tombs and three vaults including a large 19th-century mausoleum of the MacDonagh family.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
A mill is indicated in this townland adjacent to the E townland and barony boundary on the Down Survey (1655-6) barony map and in the general area of Kilmorgan church (SL034-081001-). The precise location of it is not known but it may be on or close to the location of a T-shaped mill which is indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map immediately to S of the road leading W from Cams Bridge. There are no visible remains of any structure in the area which is densely covered with overgrowth. The remains of a probably associated rectangular structure (c. 3.6m NW-SE; 6m SW-NE) lie c. 10m to SW. This structure is defined by a hollow with a rising scarp on the SE and NE sides, the remains of the SW wall built against a rock-face and a short section of the NW wall (L 2.1m; H 2m; T 0.73m) with a central lintelled door (Wth 0.76m). The faint trace of an embanked millrace curves around the structure to S and E. Kilmorgan church (SL034-081001-) lies c. 50m to S.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on an upland terrace on the lower NE-facing slopes of Kesh Corann Hill. A large mound (20m N-S; 16m E-W), the centre of which has been quarried leaving a rim (H 3m) around a central irregular hollow (diam. 10m). A break at E gives access to the grassed-over quarry pit. The mound appears to be primarily earthen in composition but incorporates some stone. A slight depression NE-SE may indicate a silted-up fosse (Wth 4m). At E, a low berm-like feature between the fosse and the mound may be due to the disturbance of the mound as it is located in the area of the access gap into the quarry pit. A field boundary skirts the base of the mound at W. A circular enclosure (SL040-003002-) lies 2m to N and a rath (SL040-004----) c. 40m to S.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
(In the Carrowkeel-Kesh Corann passage tomb cemetery). On a spur on the northern slopes of Kesh Corann and commanding an extensive outlook to the N. A NE-facing passage tomb (L 5m) stands towards the N end of a ruined circular cairn (diam. 19m; H c. 0.5m). Some kerbstones at the W side of the cairn and one or two possible examples at the E indicate an original diameter of c. 15m. Eight orthostats form the more easterly side of the tomb. There are four, possibly five, in situ at the opposite side and it is closed by a substantial backstone. An in-turn of the more easterly side divides the tomb into an inner (L 3m; max. Wth 1.5m) and outer (L 2m) compartment. A large roofstone (max. dim. 2.5m) is in place above the inner compartment. A much smaller stone wedged between the forward end of the last and the more westerly side of the tomb may be a displaced roofstone. A large slab (max. dim. 2.1m) leans against the outer face of the more westerly side of the outer compartment and would seem to be a displaced roofstone. Ten or more relatively small slabs lie displaced at the site. In 1993 a small pocket of cremated bone, apparently a secondary deposition, found near the kerb was later identified as the remains of one adult (Buckley and Mount 1994, 71). An enclosure (SL040-00602-) lies immediately to S. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 84)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
On the N end of a spur of Kesh Corann and immediately S of a passage tomb (SL040-006001-). A roughly D-shaped area (26.5m N-S; 29m E-W) enclosed by remnants of a stone wall (Wth 2m; H 0.3m) which survives as low sod-covered hummocks from which large stones protrude. The wall can be traced in a broad curve WNW-S and at N it merges with the sod-covered base of the passage tomb cairn, appearing to post-date the cairn. A natural rocky scarp defines the straight W side of the enclosure. The enclosure encompasses most of the level ground on the top of the spur.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

On a rocky spur on the lower NE-facing slopes of Kesh Corann and immediately W of Poulagaddy cave (SL040-006003-). A subcircular area (5m E-W; 4.8m N-S) defined by a 'wall' of single contiguous moss-covered stones. This 'wall' is best defined S-NW but there are breaks at N and SE. The interior slopes gently down to NW. A subrectangular arrangement (c. 6m E-W; c. 5m N-S) of mostly widely spaced stones, sharing its W side with the hut site, was noted immediately to the E, surrounding the entrance to the cave.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In undulating pasture, on top of a ridge, and within a small field. A circular area (int. diam. 29m) enclosed by two earthen banks and an intervening fosse. The inner bank (Wth 3m; int. H 0.8m; ext. H 2.2m) is evident all round. The intervening fosse has been widened (Wth 4m; D 1.2m) due to quarrying along the SW arc. The outer bank (Wth 3m; int. H 1.4m; ext. H 1m) is best preserved along the S arc and is mostly levelled elsewhere. There is a possible entrance (Wth 1m) through the inner bank at SE with a corresponding ramped causeway across the fosse. The OS 6-inch maps show that the rath was enclosed by field boundaries between 1838 and 1913. Recorded in 1836 as 'Doorly Fort' (OSNB vol. 2, 229).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In the Owenmore River. This monument was listed as ‘Weir’ in the SMR (1989) and RMP (1995). This is one of seven records for weirs (SL026-122----; SL026-126-----; SL026-130----; SL026-159-----; SL026-159001-; SL026-159002-; SL026-159003-) recorded in the SMR whose only source is noted as ‘Marked on estate map dated 1618’ (SMR file). It has not proved possible to identify this map. It is marked and named ‘Fish Weir’ on the 1837 edition of the OS 6-inch map; it is named ‘Eel Weir’ on the 1913 edition. On inspection in 1992 two upright posts, c. 15m apart, were noted in the middle of the river. It is likely that other residual elements survive on the river bed. Although the date of this weir is unknown the possibility that it pre-dates 1700 AD cannot be ruled out.

Compiled by: Paul Walsh

Date of upload: 18 October 2011

source_data.original_text:
Not listed in either the SMR (1989) or RMP (1995). This limekiln is cut into N-facing hillside in a small limestone quarry. The limekiln comprises rubble limestone walls laid in rough courses and bonded with a gravely lime mortar. The front elevation (H 3.2m) faces NNE, with a wooden lintelled recess (H 1.6m; D 1.65m) and a stepped lower lintel with a supporting wooden and iron bar. The rear of the recess consists of stepped stones with an ope at the base which is blocked with rubble. The bottom of funnel (diam. 2.1m) is infilled with rubble. This is probably post-1700 AD in date.


Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC

Date of upload: 04 January 2012

source_data.original_text:
Not listed in either the SMR (1989) or the RMP (1995). Not shown on any edition of the OS 6-inch map. In pasture, on the W side of a road. A mid/late 19th-century limekiln which is built against the slope. This is a rectangular structure (3.3m N-S; 5.4m E-W) with rounded corners, inclining inwards with height. Random rubble limestone walls encase an earthen core. The front elevation (H c. 4m) faces N and has a stone-lintelled recess (Wth 1.65m; H 1.8m; D 2m) supported by a wooden pole. The recess is stepped down towards the rear and there is a narrow rectangular ope at the base. The funnel is infilled but its position is indicated by a circular depression (diam. 2m; D 1.5m). There is a low earthen ramp to rear. A small yard area in front of the recess is defined by a scarp on the E side and a stone wall on the W side. This is probably post-1700 AD in date.


Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC

Date of upload: 04 January 2012

source_data.original_text:
In undulating pasture, just off the summit of a N-S ridge which affords panoramic views. Part of a small barrow cemetery consisting of another bowl-barrow (SL033-039002-) with an adjacent ring-barrow (SL033-039003-) c. 30m to N. This bowl-barrow consists of a prominent conical grass-covered mound (diam. 24.5m x 23.5m; H 6.1m). A resistivity survey identified an extensive fosse enclosing the site (Mount 1995a, 81). Subsequent excavation in 1994 and 1995 (Mount 1996, 78-9) confirmed the presence of the fosse (Wth 6.7m; D 2.1m) and also revealed an external bank (Wth 2.4m) and a large displaced limestone boulder, probably a kerbstone. Preserved seeds from the lower fill of the fosse were radiocarbon dated to 3930-3520 cal. BC, placing the construction of the barrow in the earlier part of the Neolithic period (Mount 1998, 18).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In gently undulating pasture, on top of a steep-sided flat-topped rock outcrop. A slightly raised oval area (36m N-S; 29m E-W) defined by an earth and stone bank, a rock-cut scarped edge and a natural cliff. The earth and stone bank (int. H 0.3m; ext. H 2.45m) encloses the interior SE-WSW, with the entrance (Wth 2m) and a ramp to the exterior at SSW. A near vertical cliff-face (ext. H c. 4.5m) defines the interior from WSW-NW and is topped by a low stone wall WNW-NW which extends along the line of the cliff to N beyond the cliff-edge fort. This low wall (int. H 0.3m) consists of limestone slabs (average dims. 0.4m x 0.5m x 0.2m) set on edge. A vertical rock-cut scarp (ext. H 0.2-0.4m) defines the interior NW-SE. A number of small rock quarries are located at NW, N and E of the scarp. These quarries are angular in plan and are no deeper than the height of the scarped edge where they are located. A crescent-shaped area (Wth 14m N-S), being the summit of the rock outcrop outside the enclosing element, lies to the N of the cliff-edge fort NW-SE. A near vertical cliff-face (H c. 6m) defines the limit of this area. The interior of the cliff-edge fort slopes gently down to S and is flat and clear of overgrowth. There is a souterrain (SL033-022002-) in the NW quadrant.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on the spine of a N-S ridge which affords panoramic views. Part of a small barrow cemetery consisting of an adjacent ring-barrow (SL033-039003-) immediately to W and another larger bowl-barrow (SL033-039001-) c. 30m to S. This bowl-barrow consists of a conical oval grass-covered mound (diam. 9m at base; H 3.5m) enclosed by a fosse (Wth 3.3m; D 0.4m). A resistivity survey indicated the presence of an outer bank (Mount 1995a, 81). Partial excavation in 1995 (Mount 1996, 78-9) revealed that the mound was constructed of clay, silt and sand with occasional cut sods and contained an iron fragment, animal and human bones and charcoal. The mound was revetted by a single course of stone kerbing (ibid.). It was also determined that the mound was built on top of scorched earth, probably resulting from the lighting of a funeral pyre and wood from the base of the fosse was radiocarbon dated to 380-120 cal. BC, giving an Iron Age date (Mount 1998, 21). The excavation also determined that the adjacent ring-barrow (SL033-039003-) was built onto the existing bowl-barrow creating a figure-of-eight monument (ibid.).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, located on an expanse of relatively level ground, with gently rising ground immediately to W, and a slight fall of ground to E. There is a stream c. 100m to E and a spring well c. 100m to N. Views of the surrounding landscape are now largely obscured by trees planted on the borders of the field, and by a forestry planation to N. Nevertheless, the cairn-topped peaks of the Ox Mountain range can be glimpsed in the distance to N, with the landmark silhouette of Ben Bulben beyond, and visible on the far horizon to S are the passage tomb-topped limestone ridges of Carrowkeel, and to SE, the looming outline of Kesh Corann, crowned by its cairn (SL040-008----).
MacDonagh (1936, 198) records the tradition of a church, located near Newport House in 'a field called Killack, the church of the flagstones. The church, however, has totally disappeared. The people of the locality say that the field was an old burial ground, and for that reason are afraid to pass through it after dark.' 
There are no visible traces of a church (SL033-167----) or graveyard (SL033-167001-), but the levelled outline of a large circular enclosure (SL033-167002-) can be traced at ground level. According to local information, this enclosure is the site traditionally known as ‘Killack’ (pers. comm. Anthony Kitchen, November 2017). 
The enclosure consists of a very slightly raised, circular area (diam. 91m E−W; 87m N−S) defined by a low, broadly sloping scarp (Wth 3-4m; ext. H 0.5-0.6m), representing a levelled bank. The scarp remains relatively well defined NW−S, but at SW−NE it is reduced to a barely discernible undulation. There is low area or possible break (Wth c. 3m) at NW. The ground (Wth c. 4m) immediately outside the scarp at S−SW is damp and marked by rushes and yellowish grass. This might indicate the presence of an enclosing fosse, however, it cannot be traced elsewhere around the circuit. The interior has a very slight slope from W down to E, and is grass-covered and featureless. An old quarry pit (c. 20m N−S; c. 15m E−W; D 1-1.5m) abuts the SE edge of the enclosure, partly truncating the enclosing scarp. A post-and-wire fence extends across the N end of the enclosure on a NE−SW axis.
The large size of this enclosure, coupled with the local traditions of a church, graveyard and the placename ‘Killack’, suggests the possibility that this is an Early Medieval ecclesiastical enclosure. There is a cliff-edge fort (SL033-022001-) located 725m to W. Another large circular enclosure (SL033-077001-), with a diameter of c. 100m, is located c. 1.5km to SW.

source_data.original_text:
In undulating pasture, on the top of a limestone bluff in the SW-facing foothills of the Bricklieve Mountains. A broadly oval area (int. diam. 30.1m NW-SE; 24.2m NE-SW) enclosed by a substantial ruined stone wall (Wth 4m; int. H 0.8m; ext. H 1m). Large limestone boulders protruding from the bank may be remains of external stone facing. From W-NW the outer edge of the stony bank coincides with a low natural scarp of limestone. A few metres to W there is an abrupt drop (H c. 4m) at the base of which is flat wet pasture. From E-SE are remains of a field boundary wall (Wth c. 1m) grafted onto the external face of the stone bank and rising c. 0.4m above it. A low berm-like stony spread (Wth 2m; H 0.4m) skirts the base of the stone bank SE-WSW. The interior is level and grass-covered. There is a possible entrance (Wth 2m) at E. Another cashel (SL040-146----) lies 24m to ENE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, located on a level terrace on the steep W-facing slope of a limestone ridge, on the W flank of the Bricklieve Mountains. The slope rise immediately to E of the cashel to a low exposed limestone cliff face, then rises again in a series of terraces and limestone escarpments to the ridge summit, which is crowned by a cairn (SL040-103----), c. 375m to SE. The terrace overlooks a small valley of damp pasture, with extensive views beyond to SW−W of a broad sweep of undulating countryside. Kesh Corran looms at NW.
One of two conjoined cashels; the second cashel (SL040-083002-) lies immediately to N. This cashel consists of a broadly oval area (28m E−W; 21.5m N−S) defined by remnants of a wall. The wall is evident as a low, moss-covered stony rise (Wth 1.5-2m; H 0.2-0.4); stones can be glimpsed or felt beneath the moss and sod, but no intact section of wall structure is visible. The cashel encompasses the full E−W width of the terrace, with the E arc cut into the rising slope, creating an inward-facing scarp (H 1-1.2m), and the W arc merging with the break of slope at the edge of the terrace, where ground falls away steeply. The N arc of the enclosing wall, which is shared with the second cashel (SL040-083002-), appears more substantial (Wth 3m; H 0.5m), but this is largely because it is overlain by a later E-W field wall, which is also ruined and moss-covered. 
The interior has a very slight slope down to W, reflecting the natural incline of the terrace. There is a souterrain (SL040-083001-) in the SW quadrant. The souterrain consisting of a length of collapsed passage, evident as a linear depression (L 10.5m), with several exposed and displaced roofing lintels tipping into it. It extends on a NE-SW axis from close to the cashel wall at SW to the centre of the interior. Immediately to W of the souterrain there is a slight rise in interior ground level. Remnants of a wall, visible as a low, moss-covered stony rise, extend from the NE end of the souterrain to the cashel wall at E; this wall may post-date the cashel.
Adjacent to the enclosing wall in the SE quadrant there is a line of moss-covered stony hummocks (L 2-3m E−W), possible a wall remnant of some kind of structure or internal division of the cashel –but this is very uncertain. There is another moss covered concentration of stones (c. 2m across) close to the enclosing wall at S, also of uncertain significance. Barely discernible linear cropmarks, on an E−W axis, are visible throughout the interior, and are suggestive of ridge and furrow cultivation.
The location of the original entrance is unclear: there a small break (Wth c. 1m) in the enclosing wall at S and another at SW, and at NW there may have been a gap allowing access to the other cashel, but all are poorly defined and uncertain.
Two large close-set slabs, one clearly edge-set in the ground, are located 2m outside the cashel wall at S; it is possible that they are related to the cashel, but they may simply be remnants of an E−W field wall.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy 

Date of upload: 24 April 2018

source_data.original_text:
Bóthar an Corann or Bothar na Slieve connected the town of Ballymote, Co. Sligo with Boyle, Co. Roscommon by a route around the SW side of Kesh Corran and to the W of the Bricklieve Mountains, a distance of c. 20km. According to Timoney and Timoney (2001, 21), Richard de Burgh, the Red Earl of Ulster, is credited with building this road to get from his castle at Ballymote (SL033-092----) into Roscommon. This entry deals only with that part of the road in Co. Sligo, i.e. from close to Ballymote as far as the Roscommon border. The road traverses a number of townlands over a number of the 1914 edition of the OS 6-inch sheets: OS 33: Ardsallagh/ Corhober/Mullaghcor; 
OS 39: Ardsallagh/Knocknacroy/Cross/Cloonagh/ Knocknawhishoge; 
OS 40:Carrowreagh/Dernaskeagh; OS 45: Meenmore/ Derrygolagh/Dernaskeagh. A possible link road between Bothar an Corann and Bothar an Iarla Ruaid (SL033-147---) goes from Greenan townland, around the S side of the Bricklieve Mountains, to Ballinafad.

Sections of Bóthar an Corann are recorded as five separate records (SL033-145---; SL039-031----; SL040-143----; SL040-153----; SL045-002----) commencing at Ballymote and following the route SE to the county boundary with Roscommon. Only sections of the road are indicated on these maps though it was, of course, continuous.

This section (SL040-153----) traverses the townlands of Dernaskeagh and Derrygolagh. The portion in Dernaskeagh zig-zags gently for a distance of c. 0.5km in a NW direction through poorly drained pasture, then swings to WNW for a further 0.4km cutting across the lower SSW-facing slope of the hill. It is evident for most of this section as a very shallow linear depression (Wth c. 4.5m). A short section has been incorporated into a farm trackway and is bounded by post-and-wire fencing. Close to the point where the trackway changes direction to WNW it becomes difficult to trace and a short section appears to coincide with the line of a modern road. Continuing to WNW it cuts into the slope of the hill where it takes the form of a sunken way (Wth 4m) bordered on the N side by a vertical S-facing scarp (H 0.9m), roughly revetted in places with stone, cut into the rising slope of the hill, and on the S side by a substantial earth and stone field boundary. A shallow drain (Wth 0.9m) is cut into the base of the trackway along the inner face of the field boundary. The section is covered with overgrowth of hazel, holly, bushes and brambles. A single test-trench dug at the S end of this section in 2001 (at ITM grid reference 573245, 807214) revealed a trackway (Wth c. 2.5m) consisting of 'woven timbers, 20mm to 40mm wide laid on east/west and north/south axes, with the runners orientated north/south' c. 0.45m below the present surface (Read 2001a). The trackway appeared to lie in a natural hollow or possible cut and the eastern and western edges seemed to be defined by medium sized stones (ibid.). A deposit of burnt material was also revealed on one side of the trackway (Read 2003, 358).
To the S of this the road extends on a roughly NNW-SSE axis for a furtherv c. 1km, crossing the townland boundary into Derrygolagh. It is poorly preserved and does not survive as a continuous track. It is mostly evident as a shallow, linear, waterlogged depresssion (Wth c. 4m; D 0.3-0.5m) bordered by traces of parallel banks or, where cut into rising ground, by low scarps. In places it is very difficult to trace, being evident only as a slight surface indentation , or makred by a dense growth of rushes.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

Date of revision: 1 June 2011

source_data.original_text:
Bóthar an Corann or Bothar na Slieve connected the town of Ballymote, Co. Sligo with Boyle, Co. Roscommon by a route around the SW side of Kesh Corran and to the W of the Bricklieve Mountains, a distance of c. 20km. According to Timoney and Timoney (2001, 21), Richard de Burgh, the Red Earl of Ulster, is credited with building this road to get from his castle at Ballymote (SL033-092----) into Roscommon. This entry deals only with that part of the road in Co. Sligo, i.e. from close to Ballymote as far as the Roscommon border. The road traverses a number of townlands over a number of the 1914 edition of the OS 6-inch sheets: OS 33: Ardsallagh/ Corhober/Mullaghcor; 
OS 39: Ardsallagh/Knocknacroy/Cross/Cloonagh/ Knocknawhishoge; 
OS 40:Carrowreagh/Dernaskeagh; OS 45: Meenmore/ Derrygolagh/Dernaskeagh. A possible link road between Bothar an Corann and Bothar an Iarla Ruaid (SL033-147---) goes from Greenan townland, around the S side of the Bricklieve Mountains, to Ballinafad.

Sections of Bóthar an Corann are recorded as five separate records (SL033-145---; SL039-031----; SL040-143----; SL040-153----; SL045-002----) commencing at Ballymote and following the route SE to the county boundary with Roscommon. Only sections of the road are indicated on these maps though it was, of course, continuous.

This section (SL045-002----) (L c. 150m) is indicated on 1914 OS 6-inch map by two broken parallel lines. There are no visible remains of the NW end of this section (L c. 100m) which has been covered by an extensive tract of forestry. The remaining 50m of the trackway is evident as a shallow depression (Wth c. 2m) cut into the S-facing hillslope. Towards the NW end it is bordered by a slight scarping of the hillslope on the uphill side and by remnants of a bank on the downhill side. The SE end terminates at a stream which is crossed by stepping-stones at that point. The road may have continued on the S side of the stream (though this is not indicated on the OS 6-inch maps) and this area is now covered with forestry.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

Date of revision: 1 June 2011

source_data.original_text:
In the SE corner of a drained lake; the extent of the lake is marked by a growth of rushes. Views are restricted by surrounding drumlins though Kesh Corann is visible in the distance. A roughly circular low-mound crannog (diam c. 31m; H 1.8m) sloping down gently to indistinct edges. There is an oval elevation (15.2m N-S; 11.9m E-W; H c. 0.35m) in the E portion. An old N-S drain cuts through this elevation revealing layers of sand flecked with charcoal as well as some evenly sized stones (dims. 0.3m x 0.2m). A more recent drain also cuts through the crannog, skirting the W edge of the elevation. This reveals that the crannog sits on lake sand, over which is a layer of peat containing horizontal timbers, roundwood and some brushwood. On top of this is a thin layer of fire-cracked stones.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In lowlying, rush-grown pasture on the N shore of Templevanny Lough.
Visible as a very low, subcircular rise or mound (diam. c. 15m; H 0.3m), with an irregular, undulating sod-covered surface. The mound has a clearly defined sloping edge at E−S, but merges gradually with the surrounding ground elsewhere. A few large stones (max. dim. 0.2-0.3m) protrude from the surface on the NW edge. The mound feels firm and compact underfoot, which contrasts with the softer, damper surrounding ground. Probing revealed a concentration of limestone fragments in a dark, peaty soil. While it was unclear if the soil contained charcoal fragments, it appeared darker in colour to the peaty soil in the surrounding field. There are a number of shallow, surface dips or depressions, but none that could be interpreted with certainty as indicating the location of a trough. It is located 6m N of the current lake shore, but may have been closer to the water’s edge or even inundated in times past.
This may be the remains of a burnt mound. Or it may a lakeshore settlement feature; in this light it is interesting to note a crannog (SL040-147----) located on the W shore of the lake, 85m to SW. There is also a possibility that the mound relates to some more recent farming or land reclamation activity.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 6 July 2018

A D-shaped area (dims. 23m WNW-ESE; min. 20m NNE-SSW) defined on the straight NW side by a field boundary wall and a road and ENE-W by a shallow fosse with an external bank. The road probably truncates the rath. The shallow fosse (Wth 2m; D 0.3m) is a poorly defined depression of damp ground, marked by a growth of rushes. The bank (Wth 5.5m; int. H 0.5m; ext. H 0.3m) is evident as a low rise with a well-defined inner face bordering the fosse but with a broad low external slump. It is best preserved E-S, becoming increasingly degraded S-W. There is a break (Wth 4.4m) in the bank at S with a causeway (Wth c. 3m) across the fosse. The interior is level but has a slight depression (diam. 7m) in the W half.

A subrectangular graveyard (c. 60m NW-SE; c. 50m NE-SW), with a recent extension to E, enclosed by a stone wall and containing many 19th- and 20th-century grave-plots marked with limestone headstones. There are no visible remains of the of the possible church (SL040-14801-) which was reported here in 1836 (OSL, 151). In the graveyard is a 17th-century recumbent graveslab (SL040-148006-) of Thomas C. Mervin, who died in 1672 (pers. comm. M. B. Timoney). Some quernstones, metal slag and a sandstone window fragment from here are in the NMI (pers. comm. M. A. Timoney). It has also been noted (M. B. Timoney 2001b, 54) that the memorials in the graveyard are arranged in a curving pattern, possibly indicating the former existence of a possible circular ecclesiastical enclosure (SL040-148004-).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In undulating rocky pasture. This short cist was found in the centre of a mound barrow (SL040-15501-), c. 0.3m below the surface and c. 4.5m from a pit-burial (SL040-15502-). It was discovered in 1970 during sand extraction and investigated by E. Rynne (Raftery 1973, 186-7). The cist seemed to have been originally polygonal in plan (L 0.6m; Wth 0.45m; D 0.43m) with four of the sides composed of single slabs (T 3.5-8cm) and the fifth of drystone-walling, floored by a single slab and covered by two capstones, one on top of the other. The spaces between the tops of the sides and the lower capstone were filled with small flat stones. The cremated remains of an adult were found beside a decorated bowl food vessel (H 14.3cm; ext. rim diam. 16cm; int. rim diam. 13.5cm) which stood mouth upwards in one corner. A scatter of cremated bone was recovered from amongst stones around the N side of the capstones. Fragments of charcoal including oak and hazel were found under the floor slab. The food vessel (see photograph in M. A. Timoney 2002c, 102) is now in the National Museum of Ireland. (Waddell 1990, 131-2; Ó Ríordáin and Waddell 1993, 130)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In a cashel (SL040-083----). This souterrain (SL040-083001-) is located in the SW quadrant of the cashel. It consists of a length of collapsed passage, evident as a shallow, grassed-over linear depression (L 10.5m; Wth 2-3m; D 0.7-1m), with several exposed and displaced roofing lintels tipping into it. It extends on a NE−SW axis from close to the cashel wall at SW to the centre of the interior. Glimpses of intact drystone walling can be seen in parts on the SE side of the passage, but the NW side is low, slumped and entirely sod-covered. At least seven massive limestone roofing lintels remain more or less in place. A few are close-set or contiguous, but there are large gaps between others. The E end of some lintels are still in situ, resting on intact sections of the drystone wall on the SE side of the passage;the opposite ends are collapsed into the base of the passage.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

source_data.original_text:
Located on a level terrace on the steep W-facing slope of a limestone ridge, on the W flank of the Bricklieve Mountains. The slope rise immediately to E of the cashel to a low exposed limestone cliff face, then rises again in a series of terraces and limestone escarpments to the ridge summit, which is crowned by a cairn (SL040-103----), c. 375m to SE. The terrace overlooks a small valley of damp pasture, with extensive views beyond to SW−W of a broad sweep of undulating countryside. Kesh Corran looms at NW.
One of two conjoined cashels; the other cashel (SL040-083----) lies on the S side. This cashel consists of a broadly oval area (22m E−W; 18.6m N−S) defined by remnants of a wall. The wall is evident as a low, moss-covered stony rise (Wth 1.5-2m; H 0.2-0.4); stones can be glimpsed or felt beneath the moss and sod, but no intact section of wall is visible. The cashel encompasses the full E−W width of the terrace, with the E arc cut into the rising slope, creating an inward-facing scarp (H 1-1.2m). At SE−SW the enclosing wall is shared with the second cashel (SL040—083---) and is overlain by remnants of a later E−W field wall. At SW−NW, the wall coincides with the break of slope at the edge of the terrace, where ground falls away steeply. The N arc is gapped; it is poorly preserved at NW, but somewhat better preserved at N−NE. There is a gap (Wth 3m) at N, which may be an original entrance; however, it opens onto a narrow, shallow depression or trench (Wth 1-1.5m; D 0.3-0.4m), which extends from the gap into the interior to S for 4m. The function of this depression is unclear; there is no definitive evidence to suggest that it is part of a souterrain.
The cashel interior is level. A remnant of an E−W wall extends through the interior. It can be traced as a slight mossy rise (Wth c. 1m; H 0.1-0.2m), extending from the enclosing wall at W for 5-6m to E toward the centre of the interior. There is a low, moss-covered rise (L c. 2m E−W), of uncertain significance, just S of centre. Barely discernible cropmarks on an E-W axis throughout the interior may be the remnants of cultivation ridges. At SW there is a low section/possible gap in the enclosing wall shared with the conjoined cashel (SL040-083----), which might represent an access point between the two cashels, but this is uncertain.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy 

Date of upload: 25 April 2018

In upland pasture, in a natural hollow on the N-facing slope of a knoll in the Bricklieve Mountains and within the N end of a field system (SL040-063001-). A slightly sunken circular area (4.7m E-W; 3.7m N-S) defined by a low stone bank (Wth 1.8m; int. H 0.4m; ext. H 0.5m) with the remnants of internal stone facing. At N and S, where the bank is scarped into rising ground, it has a vertical internal face (H 0.75m) and a slight external lip. Immediately to W of the hut site the hollow has been quarried for limestone producing a U-shaped pit (10.4m E-W; 7.4m N-S) defined on the S, W and N by vertical sides (H 1.5m) of exposed limestone. The hut site is located at the edge of the open E end of this pit and the base of the pit is at a slightly lower level than that of the hut. A cairn (SL040-066----) lies c. 17m to S on the summit of the knoll.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In upland pasture, at a break of slope on the steep NW side of a ridge in the Bricklieve Mountains. The rath lies within a field system (SL040-063001-). It consists of an oval platform (48m NE-SW; 53.5m NW-SE) defined NE-S by an earthen bank (Wth 4m; ext. H 1.6m) with a low internal lip (int. H 0.4m) and elsewhere by a well defined scarp (H 1.6m). A shallow external fosse (Wth 3m; D 0.6m) is evident all round. A degraded counterscarp bank (Wth c. 2m; ext. H 0.2m) is evident W-SE. A NW-SE field boundary wall truncates the counterscarp bank and the outer edge of the fosse SW-W. The centre of the interior appears slightly domed in profile and traces of cultivation ridges are evident in the NE quadrant. Close to the scarp at S is a small circular depression (3m E-W; 2m N-S; D 0.5m) marked by thistles. A deeper linear pit (9m NE-SW; 2-3m NW-SE; D 1m) cuts through the top of the scarp at SW and extends into the interior. Some quarrying of the scarp face has occurred NNW-NE. There are several breaks in the bank and the scarp due to erosion by farm stock. A possible entrance (Wth 2.3m) is at ENE with a ramp-like slope to an infilled section of the fosse and a corresponding break (Wth 4m) in the counterscarp bank. A possible rath (SL040-233----) lies c. 16m to SE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In undulating pasture. An oval flat-topped knoll (c. 60m NE-SW; c. 80m NW-SE; H c. 6m) with a terraced profile. The terracing appears to be natural, determined to some extent by rock outcrops. The knoll is an extension of a broader ridge that stretches to NW and it projects from the ridge into an expanse of flat, poorly drained ground. The flat top (29m NW-SE; 10m NE-SW) is defined by a natural limestone scarp (H 2m). From this platform, the knoll drops in a series of terraces to the base. The terraces are narrow (Wth 6m) at NE and SW but expand to 16m at SE side. A small roughly circular sod-covered stony rise (diam. 10m) is evident on the broad lower terrace (16m NW-SE) at SE. A flat-topped spine (Wth 4.5m NE-SW) of elevated ground extending for 21m to NW from the NW end of the knoll, forms a causeway-like link to the higher main ridge. It appears to be naturally raised but with sides (H 0.7-1.2m) that may be artificially scarped. A scarp along the base of the knoll SE-W may be recent and associated with remnants of a field boundary wall that skirts the knoll. Kingstown well (SL040-138----) lies c. 100m to E.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, at the base of a slope. An unenclosed spring well, covered with overgrowth, and with an ash tree growing out of it. In 1836 it was recorded that there was formerly a 'station' at the well on every Easter Sunday (OSL, 149) while in 1942-4 it was noted that there had been no pilgrimages in the memory of the oldest resident (ITA). There is a local tradition that St Patrick threw a stone from Toomour (SL040-140001-) and the spring rose from where it fell (pers. comm. M. A. Timoney). Also according to local information, c. 30 rounded stones (max. diam. c. 0.3m) from this well were built into the wall outside a public house in Knockoconor townland c. 1.3km to NW (pers. comm. M. A. Timoney). A stretch of the road known as Bothar an Corann (SL033-145----) is c. 40m to the SW. Another holy well called 'Tobernamulla' (SL040-133----) is c. 420m to NW.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
Bóthar an Corann or Bothar na Slieve connected the town of Ballymote, Co. Sligo with Boyle, Co. Roscommon by a route around the SW side of Kesh Corran and to the W of the Bricklieve Mountains, a distance of c. 20km. According to Timoney and Timoney (2001, 21), Richard de Burgh, the Red Earl of Ulster, is credited with building this road to get from his castle at Ballymote (SL033-092----) into Roscommon. This entry deals only with that part of the road in Co. Sligo, i.e. from close to Ballymote as far as the Roscommon border. The road traverses a number of townlands over a number of the 1914 edition of the OS 6-inch sheets: OS 33: Ardsallagh/ Corhober/Mullaghcor; 
OS 39: Ardsallagh/Knocknacroy/Cross/Cloonagh/ Knocknawhishoge; 
OS 40:Carrowreagh/Dernaskeagh; OS 45: Meenmore/ Derrygolagh/Dernaskeagh. A possible link road between Bothar an Corann and Bothar an Iarla Ruaid (SL033-147---) goes from Greenan townland, around the S side of the Bricklieve Mountains, to Ballinafad.

Sections of Bóthar an Corann are recorded as five separate records (SL033-145---; SL039-031----; SL040-143----; SL040-153----; SL045-002----) commencing at Ballymote and following the route SE to the county boundary with Roscommon. Only sections of the road are indicated on these maps though it was, of course, continuous.

This section (SL040-143----) of the road (L c. 1.2km) is not visible at ground level but the its circuit can be followed by the course of a drainage channel.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

Date of revision: 1 June 2011

source_data.original_text:
Not included in the SMR (1989) but listed in the RMP (1995) and classified 'House Site'. Not shown on the 1838 edition of the OS 6-inch map. In pasture, on an E-facing slope overlooking Lough Gowra. Upon inspection in 1994 The remains of a rectangular stone-built house (L 8m; Wth 2.8m) were identified. The walls (T 0.95m; int. H 0.45m; ext. H 0.3m) are sod-covered and composed of stones bedded on their sides. A door ope (Wth 0.45m) is on the NW side. A limekiln is indicated on the 1838 map c. 40m to the E. (SMR file). On a re-inspection in 2002 no remains of this house could be found. However, 20m to SE are the foundations of another rectangular house (11.4m E-W; 5.2m N-S) divided internally into two rooms of unequal size. Yet another house lies 11m to S connected to the previous one by a ruined wall. These are all likely to be 18th/19th century in date.

In upland pasture, at a break of slope on the steep NW side of a ridge in the Bricklieve Mountains and within a field system (SL040-06301-). source_data.original_text:
On a slight terrace on the S slope of Kesh Corann and commanding an extensive outlook to the S. This is a W-facing gallery (L 6m) which decreases in height to the E. There is a jamb-like stone at the W end of the gallery. This articulates with the N side of the structure which is now represented by at least six partly concealed orthostats. A low backstone closes the E end of the gallery. Its S side is concealed by a spread of stones and may have collapsed. A low orthostat outside the N end of the backstone may be a buttress-stone. Some 1.5m S of the backstone there are two low stones. These seem to be the remains of an outer wall. There are some remains of mound around the S half of the structure.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In rough pasture, located on a small terrace on the SE-facing slope of a ridge, overlooked immediately to NW by Kesh Corran. The ridge flanks the W side of a narrow pass, traversed now by a by-road. There is a settlement cluster (SL040-067001-) at the base of the W-facing slope of the parallel ridge, which flanks the E side of the pass. Views are blocked NW−E by higher ground, but the terrace has excellent views SE−SW over a broad sweep of undulating countryside, with a rath (SL040-069----) clearly visible on a hill top 335m to S. 
This enclosure is not shown on the 1837 and 1914 OS 6-inch maps. It consists of a roughly circular area (23m E−W; 20m N−S) defined by low remnants of a wall. The enclosure encompasses most of the level space available on the small terrace. The N arc is cut into the rising ridge slope, so that it is defined by an inward-facing scarp (H 0.8-1.4m), which is topped by the ruined, grass-covered remnants of a later E−W field wall. At NE−WNW, the enclosing wall can be traced as a low, moss-covered rise or stone bank (Wth 1m; H 0.1-0.2). At SSE−SW it coincides with the break of slope of the terrace, where the ridge slope falls away steeply. 
The interior is level. A wall, evident as a low, grass-covered stony bank (Wth 0.6-1m), extend across the S half of the interior on a roughly E−W axis. This wall must post-date the enclosure, as it appears to continue beyond the enclosure, downslope to SE. In the N half of the interior, a low, sod-covered fragment of a N−S wall extends from the scarp at N for 5-6m to S through the centre of the interior; it is possible that this is a remnant of a rectangular structure or house, but the remains are exiguous, and this interpretation is uncertain.

Attached image: SL040-247----_01.JPG: viewed from W

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 28 May 2018

In upland pasture, located on a small terrace on the SE-facing slope of a ridge, overlooked immediately to NW by Kesh Corran. The ridge flanks the W side of a narrow pass, traversed now by a by-road. There is a settlement cluster (SL040-067001-) on the lower slopes of the parallel ridge, flanking the E side of the pass. Rising ground restricts views to NW−E, but the terrace has excellent views SE−SW over a broad sweep of undulating countryside, with a rath (SL040-069----) clearly visible on a hill top 335m to S. At W ground falls away from the edge of the terrace into a small valley.
This enclosure is not indicated on the OS 6-inch maps. The remains are scant and barely discernible at ground level. The indistinct outline of a circular area (diam. 18-20m) is defined by a slight undulating rise, stony underfoot, and in parts by a cropmark/differential grass growth. On the SW arc a low stony scarp (ext. H 0.3-0.4m) can be traced. The interior area is level and not noticeably raised. A telegraph pole stands on the NW edge of the enclosure. There is another enclosure (SL040-247----) 20m to SSE on a lower terrace on the same slope.

source_data.original_text:
In undulating upland pasture, in the Bricklieve Mountains. A system of field walls, covering an area c. 500m x 300m, defines irregular and subrectangular fields adapted to the natural contours of the ridge slopes and the bedding planes of the limestone outcrop. The fields mostly hug the E-facing slopes overlooking a flat valley which contains a small lake, Lough Gowra. Within the field system is a cluster of cashels (SL040-064001-; SL040-068001-; SL040-071001-), a possible cashel (SL040-070001-), a rath (SL040-069----), a possible rath (SL040-233----), an enclosure (SL040-071002-), two cairns (SL040-066----; SL040-212----), two hut sites (SL040-063002-; SL040-063003-) and a kerb circle (SL040-072----). The field system is visible in aerial photographs (CUCAP, AVI 74-8) taken in 1968 but is now difficult to trace on the ground. A portion of it, including two possible hut sites (SL040-063002-; SL040-063003-), in the area between the cashel (SL040-068001-) and the rath (SL040-069----) has been levelled. Elsewhere the walls survive as fragmented stretches of low sod-covered jumbles of stones (Wth c. 1m). There is a hut site (SL040-065----) within the N end of the field system. The sod-covered foundations of a number of rectangular houses (L c. 8-11m; Wth 2.8-5.2m), probably of 18th or 19th-century date, are also within the field system.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on the SE-facing slope of a drumlin and c. 50m NW of a crossroads; in the N half of the older part of Drumrat graveyard (SL039-074002-) and within a possible ecclesiastical enclosure (SL039-0740010-). The outline of a rectangular church (int. c. 9.5m E-W; 5.5m N-S) is evident as grass-covered wall foundations (T c. 0.85m) on the N, E and much of the S sides. The centre of the S wall survives to a height of c. 2m and is built of rough blocks of limestone bonded with lime mortar. There are a number of grave-plots in the interior. Four cross-inscribed slabs (SL039-074006-; SL039-074011-; SL039-074012-; SL039-074013-) were located to the SE and S of the church. A fragment of a horizontal millstone (SL039-074007-) is embedded in a tomb adjacent to the external S wall. According to local tradition, this is the site of a church founded by St Feichin (OSL, 146) but the present ruin is probably that of the medieval parish church of Drumrat.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In rocky pasture, on a flat-topped rise overlooking Lough Gowra and within a field system (SL040-063001-). Conjoined along the E arc to an enclosure (SL040-071002-) which is located on a lower level. A raised oval area (int. diam. 20m x 17.2m) defined by two concentric ruinous stone walls and a short section of a third wall. The inner wall (Wth 5.2m; int. H 0.8m; ext. H 1.75m) of limestone slabs, boulders and rubble has a gap (Wth 2.8m) at N. The middle wall (Wth 1.5m; int. H 0.4m; ext. H 1.1m) forms the W arc of the conjoined enclosure and also has a gap at N. The inner and middle walls are 2m apart. An arc of outer wall (Wth 1.7m; int. H 0.4m; ext. H 0.55m) is evident 1.8m outside the middle wall SW-NW, merging with it at SW. The interior is strewn with sod-covered stones, possibly upcast from the souterrain (SL040-071003-) in the NE quadrant. A kerb circle (SL040-072----) lies c. 30m to SE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
Listed in both the SMR (1989) and RMP (1995) and classified 'Mill Possible' and 'Mill' respectively. Not indicated on any edition of the OS 6-inch map. In the bottom of a U-shaped valley, adjacent to a stream and c. 170m S of Lough Labe. A linear earthen bank (L 15m; Wth 2.9m; H 1m) and fosse (Wth 2.9m; D 0.9m) may be the remains of a millrace. The sod-covered remains of a possible structure (L 16.7m; max. Wth 7.4m) are evident to the E of the bank, on the slope down to the stream. Some burnt stone and charcoal were noted on the N side of the structure where the sod has been poached by cattle. Upslope is a linear hollow (L 13m; Wth 4m; D 2.5m) (SL040-129002-), probably the result of limestone quarrying. Its date and nature are not certain and it is possibly a post-1700 AD feature.


Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC

source_data.original_text:
In rough pasture, on a level terrace at a break of slope at the NW end of a ridge. One of a linear cluster of barrows (SL040-130001-; SL040-131----, SL040-132----). There are excellent views though it is overlooked to NW by Kesh Corann Hill. A roughly D-shaped area (4.8m NW-SE; 4.3m NE-SW) defined SE-NW by a low bank (Wth c. 1.3m; int. H 0.15m; ext. H 0.3m) with a shallow external fosse (Wth c.1m) intersecting at SW with the bank of the adjoining ring-barrow (SL040-130001-). Bordered on the straight NE side by a NW-SE field boundary. The field boundary is located on the break of slope on the NE side of the ridge and there is an abrupt steep fall of ground on its NE side. The field boundary is engulfed in dense brambles and it was impossible to determine to what extent it incorporates or truncates the barrow. There is a possible causeway (Wth 1.4m) across the fosse at SW where the bank is low, linking this barrow with the adjoining ring-barrow (SL040-130001-) though there is no corresponding low section in the bank of the latter. Listed by Farrelly and Keane (2002, 98).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a low rise at the N edge of a limestone scarp. A ruined rectangular church consisting of a nave (ext. 8m E-W; 7.5m N-S) and chancel (ext. 6.75m E-W; 5.65m N-S) with walls (T 0.8m) of roughly coursed limestone. The NW corner (H 2.3m) is intact, while the N wall of the nave is evident only as a sod-covered wall-footing incorporating the possible E jamb of a doorway ope. The N wall of the chancel is partially rebuilt and the E wall stands to a height of 1.3m. The external face of the S wall stands to a height of c. 1.5m (6-8 courses) but the internal face (H 0.7m) has largely collapsed. The W wall is partially rebuilt. A roughly constructed wall has been built against the S wall of the chancel negating the difference in width between it and the nave. The interior is covered in rubble and contains two mature sycamore trees, the bases of which are enclosed by rough stone walls. A semicircular area (c. 7.5m N-S) of stony ground was noted on the N side of the church and there is a hollow (6m N-S; 6m E-W; D 0.8m) immediately to the NW. Remnants of earthworks (SL040-135003-) are evident around the church ESE-W, some 7m from it. A ruined stone wall (Wth 0.8m) 16m to the S of it may be the remains of an enclosing element. A road (Wth 2.3m; L c. 80m) (SL040-135004-), cut into the W-facing hillslope and flanked by ruined sod-covered stone walls, approaches it from the NW. A cross-slab (SL040-135002-), known as the 'praying stone', lies 2.8m to the ENE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
A prostrate stone slab (1.13m x 0.31m; T 0.18m) lies 2.8m ENE of the NE corner of Greenan church (SL040-135001-). It was described by Herity, Kelly and Mattenberger (1997, 120) as having the 'remains of carved crosses on two faces, one part of the lower stem of a cross and the other a crudely carved cross'. The cross stem is 19cm high and 3cm wide and the crudely carved cross is 21cm high and 13cm wide (pers. comm. M. A. Timoney). This cross-slab was mentioned in 1836 as 'a large stone, which is rendered famous by curing people of a pain in the back' (OSNB vol. 2, 383). The slab is named 'Stone' on the 1838 OS 6-inch map and 'Praying stone' on the 1914 OS 6-inch map.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
Immediately to the N of Greenan church (SL040-135001-) the ground is uneven and stony and traces of the outline of a semicircular area (c. 7.5m N-S), appended to the church, are evident. To the NW of the church, and dug into the low rise on which the church stands, is an anomalous subcircular sunken area (6m N-S; 6m E-W; D 0.8m), partially infilled with stone, and with a stony rim along its N side. There is a gap (Wth 1.4m) at W and another narrower gap (Wth 0.9m) at E which has traces of possible stone facing. The nature of this feature is unclear. Immediately to the E of the chancel is a narrow strip of ground (Wth c. 7m) defined by sod-covered wall footings (Wth 0.9m) on the N and E sides. This strip extends for a short distance along the E end of the S side of the church, c. 7m S of the church where it is defined by a barely discernible rise. Outside this strip, at a distance of 16m from the church and following a natural contour, is a shallow arc (c. 44m) of a ruined wall (Wth 0.8m) ESE-W, indicated on the 1914 edition of the OS 6-inch map, that may be the remnant of a larger enclosure.

Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC with revisions by Patrick F. O'Donovan and Paul Walsh

Date of upload: 20 June 2011

source_data.original_text:
In undulating pasture, on a low rise c. 40m NE of a road; in the E side of Toomour graveyard (SL040-140004-). The ruin of a rectangular church (ext. 20.1m E-W; 7.16m N-S), the W end of which has been reduced to low sod-covered foundations. The standing walls are built of random-rubble limestone with dressed-stone quoins. In the centre of the E gable is a splayed and lintelled window embrasure, the single light of which has a pointed arch and is rebated and chamfered on its external edge. The upper portion of the internal face of this wall is beginning to collapse. Near the centre of the S wall (L 11.78m) is a small lintelled window embrasure with a square-headed light. A gap (Wth 1.8m) near the E end of this wall may mark the position of a window ope. The W wall (L 9.9m) contains no window or doorway opes. According to M. A. Timoney (2002b, 57), the W end of the church contained a room to house the resident cleric. The interior is covered by scrub overgrowth. These are the remains of the medieval parish church of Toomour. A section of Bóthar an Corann (SL033-145----) lies c. 400m to SW. There is a local tradition that St Patrick threw a stone from here and a spring rose from where it fell at the holy well (SL040-138----) (pers. comm. M. A. Timoney).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In the SW quadrant of a graveyard (SL040-140004-), recessed into a low E-facing slope. A low sod-covered cairn (5m N-S; 3m E-W; H 0.7m) with a roughly constructed E-facing drystone facade (H 0.8m) flanked by collapsed walls (Wth 0.6m; H 0.6m) that project to E for c. 3m. Immediately to the E of the facade is a slight depression (3.3m E-W; 3m N-S) containing a saint's stone (SL040-14008-). Along the top of the facade are eleven holy stones (SL040-140006-) and a perforated stone as well as two of the three cross-inscribed slabs (SL040-140005-; SL040-140009-; SL040-140010-) associated with the leacht. The leacht is known locally as the 'Grave of the Kings' (see photograph in Kilgannon 1926, 264) as it is said that following the battle of Ceis Corran in 971, all the chiefs were interred here. Some human bones were found underneath one of the cross-inscribed slabs (SL040-140009-), known as the 'Altar-table', during an exploration of the leacht, instigated by Terence O'Rorke prior to 1889 (O'Rorke [1889] vol. 2, 214).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
A raised subrectangular area (45m E-W; 26m N-S at W end; 39m N-S at E end) defined by a poorly constructed drystone wall (int. H 0.5m; ext. H 1.6m; T c. 1m). The ruin of the medieval parish church of Toomour (SL040-140001-) is located on the E side; its E wall is incorporated into the graveyard wall. The interior is grass-covered and generally level but S of the centre it slopes gently to the S. A leacht cuimhne (SL040-140003-), holy stones (SL040-140006-), three cross-inscribed stones (SL040-140005-; SL040-140009-; SL040-140010-) and a saint's stone (SL040-140008-) are in the SW quadrant. There are no visible remains of headstones or other grave-markers. The graveyard has recently been enclosed by a post-and-wire fence (pers. comm. M. B. Timoney). A bishop of 'Tuaim-fobhair' [Toomour] was ordained by St Kevin of Glendalough in the 6th century (Gwynn and Hadcock 1970, 407). There are no visible remains of any ecclesiastical enclosure around the graveyard.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
On top of a leacht cuimhne (SL040-140003-) within the SW quadrant of Toomour graveyard (SL040-140004-). Arranged in a row along the top of the E facade of the leacht cuimhne are eleven water-rolled stones (max. dim. 0.25m). Wood-Martin (1892, 366) noted seventeen of these stones and recorded that they were known locally as the 'dicket stones'. Also on top of the leacht is a sandstone block (0.3m x 0.19m; T 0.18m) with a small circular perforation (diam. 0.1m) close to one edge. The perforation has an hour-glass cross section through the thickness of the stone.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

A bishop of 'Tuaim-fobhair' [Toomour] was ordained by St Kevin of Glendalough in the 6th century (Gwynn and Hadcock 1970, 407). The outline of the N arc of this enclosure is visible on the OSI 1995 aerial photograph and it is possible that its footprint is represeneted by the field boundaries to the S of the road. Within the possible enclosure are the graveyard (SL040-140004-) and the medieval parish church of Toomour (SL040-140001-), a leacht cuimhne (SL040-140003-), on top of which is a set of holy stones (SL040-140006-), and three cross inscribed stones (SL040-140005-; SL040-140009-; SL040-040010-).

In pasture, on top of a low rise. A circular mound (7m NE-SW; 7.4m NW-SE) defined by a scarp (H 0.6m) kerbed with sod-covered upright stones. The kerbstones are mostly contiguous or close-set, though there are some gaps and a few project slightly above the level of the mound. The top of the mound is slightly sunken. Conjoined at NE is another mound (SL040-149002-). The junction of the two mounds is barely perceptible and is marked by two kerbstones which barely project above the sod. The S and SE edges of both barrows are obscured by overgrowth.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In pasture, on top of a drumlin with a commanding view. This rath is not visible at ground level. It was indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map as a D-shaped enclosure (dims. c. 30m NE-SW; straight NE side L c. 30m NNW-SSE). On the 1942-43 OS 6-inch map it was indicated as a subrectangular area (c. 40m NE-SW; c. 40m NW-SE) defined by a curving field boundary N-NE, by a curving scarp NE-SSW, by two short linear field boundaries which form a W corner and by a hachured bank NW-N. There is a souterrain (SL044-023002-) in the interior.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In Toomour graveyard (SL040-140004-), immediately to the W of a leacht cuimhne (SL040-14003-), is a large flat slab (min. dims. 1.1m x 1.1m) embedded in the ground. On its exposed surface are three, and possibly a fourth, shallow circular depressions (diam.: 0.14m; 0.16m; 0.19m; 0.3m), said to be the imprints of 'the knees of the saint of the place [probably St Luidhigh] in his constant prayers at the Altar' (O'Rorke [1889] vol. 2, 213). Also incised on this stone, close to the S edge, are three simple equal-armed crosses (dims: 0.16 x 0.15m; 0.16m x 0.14m; 0.13m x 0.14m), all 2-3cm wide, though a sketch of the stone in O'Rorke (ibid., 212) shows six crosses.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In the SW quadrant of Toomour graveyard (SL040-140004-). One of three cross-inscribed slabs (SL040-140005-; SL040-140010-) associated with the leacht cuimhne (SL040-140003-). A rectangular slab (0.47m x 0.32m; T 0.05m), on top of the leacht cuimhne, is incised with a double rectangular frame (there is a third line on one side) within which is a pattern of crossed lines described by Crawford (1913b, 165) as a 'combined cross and saltire'. O'Rorke ([1889] vol. 2, 213) recorded that this slab is known locally as the 'Altar-table' and some human bones were found under it following an exploration of the leacht cuimhne, instigated by Terence O'Rorke prior to 1889 (ibid., 214).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

On a low dry rise, in otherwise flat poorly drained ground. Kesh Corann, crowned by its cairn (SL040-008----), is visible in the distance to E. A low circular platform (11.4m E-W; H 0.3m at NE), with a slightly concave top, is defined by a fosse (Wth 3.7m) and an external bank (Wth 3.7m; int. H 0.2-0.5m; ext. H 0.3m). Moss-covered stones are visible barely protruding from the perimeter of the central platform, and from the external bank. A gap (Wth 3.8m) at N is approached from N by a linear depression (L c. 7m; Wth 3.8m). The overall diameter of the external bank is 21m. A ring-barrow (SL038-085----) lies c. 600m to ENE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In pasture, on a S-facing slope. A raised circular area (diam. 25m) enclosed by a grass-covered stone wall (Wth 2.8m; int. H 0.2m; ext. H 1m) built of large limestone blocks with a rubble core. An external terrace (Wth 8m) is defined by a scarp (H c. 1.2m) W-NW and E-SSW. Collapsed stone walls radiate out from the perimeter of the cashel to the edge of the scarp at SSW and SSE. The S half of the interior is raised c. 2m to compensate for the hillslope. There is a souterrain (SL038-061002-) in the NW quadrant of the interior. According to local information, this cashel was used as a children's burial ground (SL038-061003-).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In a cashel (SL038-061001-), located c. 2.2km WSW of Bunnanaddan. According to local information, the cashel was used as a burial ground for unbaptised children, the last known burial having taken place in the winter of 1957-8. During an inspection in December 2016, the outlines of 20-30 grass-covered graves were visible. They are rectangular, oval, subcircular or irregular-shaped in plan (sample measurement: c. 1m x c. 0.25m), and are marked by low, uninscribed field stones which barely protrude above the ground surface. A few graves are more clearly defined by low, edge-set stones. The orientation of the long axes of the graves does not appear to follow any pattern. 

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of revised upload: 17 January 2017

In pasture, on a SE-facing slope. A raised oval area (int. diam. 49m N-S; 59m E-W) enclosed by an earthen bank (Wth 3m; int. H 1.2m). A shallow external fosse (Wth 5m; D 0.05m) is evident NE-E and the line of it is indicated elsewhere, except to NW, by a 5m wide band of boggy ground. The interior is poached by cattle and there is a souterrain (SL038-083002-) in the N half. Hawthorn bushes grow on the bank. There is a small quarry immediately to NW.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In Templehouse lake, c. 200m from the N shore. A roughly circular low-cairn crannog (14m N-S; 11m E-W; H 1.4m above the soft sandy lake-bed). At the time of inspection it was submerged c. 0.4m below the water. It has an organic centre consisting of a mix of clay, mud and peat that is unstable but firm enough to walk on. There are a few flagstones and boulders laid out unevenly on the surface. The edge is defined by a slightly inward sloping stone wall consisting of loosely packed limestone stones (diam. c. 0.4m), that drops sharply down to the lake-bed. The stones form a frame for the organic interior of the site. According to local information, this crannog was built by gamekeepers from Co. Fermanagh who worked at the Templehouse estate around 1880. There is a crannog (SL033-030----) c. 200m to S.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In Templehouse lake, c. 150m from the NE shoreline. A roughly circular high-cairn crannog (23.4m N-S; 21.7m E-W; H 1.8m above the lake-bed). In the centre is a mid-cairn that blends gradually into the surrounding stony platform and berm. The crannog consists of loosely packed limestone boulders under which smaller angular stones are visible. In the N half, animal bones are mixed with the shattered stones. The edges drop gradually down into the water, though the N portion is steeper than the S portion, which gives the impression that the crannog is more easily approached from the lake. At NW a low U-shaped feature (1.4m N-S; 2.2m E-W) of large subangular stones was noted. Another crannog (SL033-029----) lies c. 200m to N and a third crannog (SL033-209----) is c. 600m to SW.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
On a promontory called 'Doon' (MacDonagh 1936, 195), jutting into Templehouse Lake. An oval raised area (int. diam. 21m E-W; 28m N-S) enclosed by two earthen banks with an intervening fosse (Wth 6.4m). The inner bank (int. H 1m; ext. H 3m) is more substantial than the outer bank (Wth 3m; int. H 1.6m; ext. H 1m). The entrance (Wth 2.5m) is at SE and has a corresponding ramp and causeway. The interior rises towards the centre giving a dome-shaped profile. MacDonagh (ibid.) recorded a cairn (SL033-04202-), called 'The Giants Grave', in the centre of this enclosure. The enclosure is partially covered by trees.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

Both chambers are high enough for an adult to stand up in, chamber 1 being at least 1.84m H and chamber 2 at least 1.7m (pers. comm. M. A. Timoney). source_data.original_text:
In shallow water in the S half of Cloonacleigha Lough. The lake is surrounded by drumlins, with views of Knocknashee and Muckelty Hill in the distance to NW and W respectively. An oval high-cairn crannog (24m N-S; 18m E-W; H 1.27m above the water). A central medium-sized mid-cairn, with a flat area of soil in the middle, is surrounded by a plateau of loosely packed angular and rounded stones interspersed with sand. In places these stones lie on top of smaller angular stones (diam. 0.1-0.15m). The E edge of the plateau is steep while the W edge spreads out evenly towards the water. A causeway at S connecting the crannog to land is visible in an aerial photograph (GSIAP, G 264-5). This causeway was not accessible from the crannog due to reeds and bog growth. The crannog itself is almost inaccessible due to overgrowth of bushes, briars and trees. There is a moated site (SL032-199----) on the shoreline c. 140m to SE (O'Conor 1998, 88; O'Sullivan 1998, pl. 52). A crannog (SL032-226----) lies c. 100m to N and another (SL033-109----) lies c. 400m to NE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In the middle of Cloonacleigha Lough, c. 100m N of another crannog (SL032-198----). The lake is surrounded by drumlins with views of the distant summits of Kesh Corann, Knocknashee and Muckelty Hill. A circular low-cairn crannog (17.8m N-S; 18m E-W; H 0.54m above the water) in the centre of which is a distinct area (6m N-S; 4.5m E-W) of stones and brown sandy soil. Around this is a plateau stretching out in all directions for c. 2m. The N edge of the crannog is marked by a semicircle of large limestone stones (diam. 0.4-0.6m). The crannog is covered by long grass. Another crannog (SL033-109----) lies c. 300m to NE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).
