source_data.original_text:
In the shallow waters of Cloonacleigha Lough, c. 70m from the N shore. An oval high-cairn crannog (25.8m N-S; 21m E-W; H c. 2m), the surface of which consists of stone packing which rises evenly over the water. The stones are loosely set and consist of rounded limestone and sandstone. Sand and gravel are evident among the more angular stones of the berm (Wth 3m). The edge drops fairly sharply into the water and down towards the lake-bed. On the S edge of the crannog is a stone jetty (4m N-S; 2m E-W) consisting of large boulders on top of smaller stones. Two crannogs (SL032-198----; SL032-226----) are c. 400m and c. 300m to SW respectively.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on top of a drumlin. A roughly oval area (64m N-S; 58m E-W) defined by remains of three earthen banks with intervening and external fosses. The inner bank (Wth 4.3m; int. H 0.4m) is evident only W-NW, elsewhere the interior is defined by a scarp (H 0.5m). The middle bank (Wth 9m; H 0.6m) is evident SW-N and E-SE and the outer bank (Wth 6.5m; H 0.3m) is evident SW-NW with a short section also at SE. The inner fosse (Wth 7m; D 0.3m) is evident all round while the middle fosse (Wth 6.5m) is evident only SE-NW. The outer fosse (Wth 5.5m; D 1.4m) is boggy and evident SW-NW. Cultivation ridges were noted in the level interior. An ENE-WSW field boundary crosses the rath. Another field boundary (on a N-S axis) clips the edge of the outer fosse at W and another (also on a N-S axis) to E is on the line of the outer bank.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In undulating poorly drained pasture, at the SW end of a natural elevation. A roughly rectangular rise (H 1.5m) with a flattened top (c. 24m NE-SW; c. 13m NW-SE) defined by a scarp on the SE, SW and NW sides. The NE side is defined by a fosse-like trench (Wth 4.7m; Wth at base 2.2m; ext. D 1.35m) on the line of a field drain and significantly wider than it. A slight undulation, 2m to NE of the drain, may indicate a levelled outer bank. On the SE side the scarp encompasses a broad natural slope (Wth c. 13m). On the SW side the scarp drops to a low spine of elevated ground extending to S for several metres, effectively an extension of the natural rise. On the NW side the scarp (Wth c. 5m) falls to an area of wet ground that may mask the line of a fosse. The interior, which encompasses the natural rise, is a relatively narrow level space, rising slightly at the SW end. Two enclosing banks and an intervening fosse are visible in an aerial photograph (IASAP, 3037081). A possible fulacht fia (SL039-006001-) lies c. 50m to NE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on top of and at the E end of a narrow ridge. A raised oval area (34.7m N-S; 29m E-W) enclosed by an earthen bank. The bank is substantial SW-NW and is lowest at E flanking the entrance (Wth 1.8m). Remains of stone facing is visible at the base of the bank, especially in the vicinity of the entrance. A break (Wth 1.5m) in the bank at N reveals a low external kerb of stones masked elsewhere by the slump of the external bank face. A band (Wth c. 3m) of soft damp ground outside the bank along the N arc probably indicates an infilled fosse. The interior is generally level but a slight E-facing scarp (H 0.1-0.2m) crossing the interior centrally on a N-S axis appears to indicate an internal division. A wide semicircular depression (Wth 7-8m E-W; ext. D 0.65m) immediately outside the bank at W is clearly the result of quarrying. The bank is thickly overgrown with hawthorn bushes.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on top of a narrow ridge with excellent views. A low subcircular platform (c. 40m N-S; c. 37.5m E-W) defined by a scarp (H 0.3m at W; 0.5m at E) from which stones protrude randomly. Set 4.5-6.5m in from the scarp edge is a wall (Wth 0.9m; H 0.8m), covered in blackthorn bushes, enclosing an oval area (28.5m N-S; 23m E-W) on the platform. At the base of the inner face of this wall from SW-N is a low terrace (Wth 2.2m) raised 0.2-0.3m above the interior ground level. In the interior, slightly NW of centre, is an ill-defined roughly circular rise (diam. 6-7m; H 0.3m). Appended to the ESE arc of the enclosure is a diamond-shaped area (40m NW-SE; 38m NE-SW) defined by a scarp (H 1.5-1.7m) with remnants of stone facing. The enclosed space encompasses the SE end of the ridge. The W half is level but it slopes gently down from the centre to ESE following the ridge slope. According to local tradition, this enclosure is known as 'Castle Ida'.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
Located on a low, dry rise in an expanse of damp, lowlying, rush-grown pasture, on the E bank of a meandering N-flowing stream. The stream lies 4-5m to W of the SW arc of the enclosure. There is a forestry plantation on the W bank of the stream. The enclosure is overlooked by a N-S ridge, located c. 100m to E, on the summit of which is a rath (SL038-062----).
This enclosure is not shown on the 1838 and 1922 OS 6-inch maps. It consists of a low, oval platform (44m E−W; 31.5m N−S) defined by a scarp (Wth of slope c. 2-3m; ext. H 0.5m, 0.8m at W) and enclosed by a fosse. The scarp is highest on the W arc of the enclosure, where the ground dips naturally to the stream. The fosse is barely discernible as a very slight depression (Wth 1-1.5m) at N−S, marked by a band (Wth c. 2m) of yellow flag iris at NW and S. The N half of the grass-covered interior appears very slightly higher than the S half. The entrance may be at E, where there is a low area (Wth 2.5-3m) in the scarp with a hint of a causeway over the fosse. 
Several roughly circular, vegetation-covered stony heaps (diam. c. 3-4; H 1m) line the edge of the stream, probably upcast material from dredging. Two of these overlie the enclosure scarp at W and SW.

source_data.original_text:
On the SW side of a holy well (SL038-120002-) and in the SE portion of a stepped barrow (SL038-120001-). An upright roughly shaped sandstone pillar (H 0.54m; Wth 0.25m; T 0.17m) with a simple cross enclosed in a ring incised on its NE face. The pillar narrows to 0.22m in width from slightly below its centre. The ring (Wth 0.25m; H 0.26m) encompasses the full width of the pillar, a double line forming the top and a single line the sides and base. The cross extends to the full width and height of the ring. Four evenly spaced linear incisions (H 0.04m) project from the upper edge of each arm of the cross. A tiny circular depression (diam. c. 15mm) flanks the shaft of the cross within the upper half of the ring. Crawford (1908, 182) has noted that this slab was brought to the Dublin Exhibition in 1907. source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on the W-facing slope of a bog-island; in the N half of an ecclesiastical enclosure (SL032-195003-). Fragmentary remains of a rectangular church (int. 19m E-W; 6.7m N-S) which, apart from its W gable with short returns of the N and S walls, has been reduced to sod-covered foundations. The surviving walling (T 1m) is built of roughly coursed limestone in a lime mortar. One window, with a flat-headed light, survives in the short return of the S wall. The SE corner stood in 1992 (SMR (1989) file) but had fallen by 2000. It contained an aumbry (Wth 0.4m; H 0.7m) and a plain round-headed piscina (H c. 0.95m), both built of limestone. There is a limestone arch-stone lying on the ground near the E end of the church. These features are all 15th/16th century in date. However, built into the E side of the window in the S wall is a single block (SL032-195005-) with Romanesque motifs including beading and cross-hatching (pers. comm. M. A. Timoney). This stone was probably a voussoir from the arch of a doorway of an earlier church. A bullaun stone (SL032-195004-) lies c. 8m to the SW of the church. There is a souterrain (SL032-194----) in the adjoining field also to the SW. A 19th-century farm building, a short distance to the NW, was built using stones derived from the church.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

raw_items.raw_text: probably on the site of a 6th-century monastery

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, at the foot of an E-facing slope, 150m SW of the Owenmore River. The roofless ruin of a rectangular church (ext. 21.5m E-W; 7.65m N-S), built of roughly coursed limestone blocks bonded by a lime mortar, with a low base-batter. A vaulted tower formerly stood at the W end but this has collapsed and its walls are reduced to the height of the side-walls and are in a very fragmentary condition. 
The church was entered through a doorway, W of the centre in the S wall, which has fallen, apart from its rear segmental arch and a drawbar-socket on the E side. Just inside it, on the W side, was a crossing-wall of which only a fragment survives. A large pile of rubble occupies the W end of the interior. The entire E gable is structurally unsound. Its central window is missing its tracery, which has recently fallen; fragments of the latter lie on the ground nearby. The light appears to have had two round sub-arches with switchline tracery above (MacDonagh n.d., vol. 18, 36). Above the light is a hood-moulding with stepped terminals. Near the E end of both the N and S walls are broken openings which may have held windows. This is the ruin of the late medieval parish church of Cloonoghill, which is probably on the site of a 6th-century monastery (Gwynn and Hadcock 1970, 377). There is no evident trace of the associated graveyard (SL033-140002-). There is a fish-pond (SL033-140004-) 30m to the SE and a dovecote (SL033-140003-) 40m to the WSW.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In pasture, on the S-facing slope of a low hill which forms a dry island in a bog. H 1m) and a narrow intervening fosse (Wth 1.2m) are evident only NE-SE, both following the indentation of the scarp. There are gaps in the bank at SSW (Wth 0.6m), SW (Wth 0.8m) and NE (Wth 1.7m). The interior is raised to compensate for the hillslope but still retains a slope down to S and SE. A circular enclosure (SL038-028003-) lies c. 20m to S in the adjoining field.

source_data.original_text:
Listed in both the SMR (1989) and RMP (1995) and classified 'Enclosure' and 'Field System' respectively. In pasture, straddling the base of a S-facing slope and c. 20m S of a rath (SL038-028001-). Indicated as a large roughly rectangular field (c. 45m E-W; c. 40m N-S) on the 1838 and 1941-2 editions of the OS 6-inch map with straight W, N and E sides and an irregular S side. The 1838 map shows the circular enclosure (SL038-028003-) partially within the SW corner of this field. The present remains consist of a large field enclosed by an earthen bank (Wth 2m) with a shallow external fosse (Wth 2m). The interior is divided in two on a N-S axis by a slightly curving E-facing scarp following a break in slope. Projecting from the S side of the field is a rectangular platform or possible house site and immediately to the E of this is a sunken trackway (Wth 3m), bordered on its E side by an earthen bank, which extends for several metres to the S. Parallel to and c. 30m W of this is a field boundary. In the intervening space are a number of low irregular hummocks, possibly the remains of houses. This is probably a 19th-century field system or deserted settlement.

source_data.original_text:
In low-lying poorly drained pasture, on the W bank of a stream. A U-shaped hollow (1.6m NW-SE; 2m NE-SW), choked with grass and rushes, cut into the SE perimeter of a stepped barrow (SL038-120001-). The hollow no longer holds water though its base is damp. A few stones protruding randomly from the edge of the hollow may be remnants of stone lining. At SE a short channel, now engulfed with irises, links the well with the adjacent stream. Mentioned as 'the well of St. Attracta' by Wood-Martin (1892, 371) who also noted that 'the "patron" held on the 11th of August at the well was abolished about the year 1776' following a faction fight at which a man was killed. He also noted that being on the borders of the county it was largely attended by Mayo and Roscommon people (ibid.). In 1942-4 it was noted that 'pilgrimages to this well have ceased and it is not now visited by anyone' (ITA) though according to local information, Mass was said here in 1990. In addition to 'stations' being performed at the well, they were also performed around a circle of hawthorn trees that grew around the adjacent barrow (Anon. 1998, no. 26). Arranged around the perimeter of the well are the following items:
(a) on the N side, a millstone (SL038-120005-)
(b) to the E of the millstone, a rectangular slab (Wth 0.42m; H 0.63m; T 0.12m) on which is carved, in relief, a cross with splayed ends. According to Wood-Martin (1892, 371), this was said to have been 'erected at the close of the last century by ''Bishop Phillips'' '.
(c) at SW, a cross-slab (SL038-120003-)
(d) at W, a 19th-century cut limestone slab (Wth 0.61m; H 0.81m; T 0.1m) which according to its inscription was erected in 1821 by John Ormsby Cooke Esq. to commemorate 'the coming of his grandfather to reside here'.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

A rectangular graveyard (51m E-W; 32m N-S), raised 0.5-1.2m above the external ground level. It contains a large number of uninscribed grave-markers and 19th- and 20th-century headstones. There is a recent extension (81m E-W; 38.5m N-S) on the W side. Fragments of a cross-slab (SL038-121003-) and of a quernstone, which were found here, are in the NMI (pers. comm. M. B. Timoney).

source_data.original_text:
On the S-facing slope of a drumlin, close to its base and flanked by a road on the SE side and in the centre of a graveyard (SL039-002002-). The remains of Cloonameehan Dominican priory consist of a rectangular church (ext. 18.7m E-W; 7.8m N-S) and a range of conventual buildings (ext. dims.: 14m N-S; 7.9m E-W) to the N, forming an overall L-shape in plan (both E walls are in line). It is built of rubble limestone set in lime mortar. The N wall of the church is entirely missing except for short sections at either end. The W gable is featureless and reduced to the height of the side-walls. The S wall stands to full height but has a major structural crack near its W end. Near its centre are the remains of a narrow window ope and near its E end is an inward-facing doorway which is missing its surround. Just short of the SE corner is a poorly preserved piscina (Wth 0.55m; H 0.8m), covered by a rounded arch with a chamfered edge, with a shallow octagonal bowl. The E gable stands to near full height. It has a central window with a double ogee-headed cusped light and a hood-moulding - the entire S jamb is missing (see Conlan 2002, fig. 11); the internal edge of the frame is moulded to house shuttering. Most of the S wall of the conventual range is missing and the other three sides stand only to ground-floor level and are missing most of their facing-stones. Enough evidence survives to show that this 2-storey range had three bluntly pointed wicker-centred E-W vaults covering its ground floor. Each vaulted bay was lit by a window in the E wall. There was also a doorway at the N end of this wall. The only possible indication of a cloister are two corbels, c. 3.5m above present ground level, on the external face of the W wall. This is the remains of a Dominican priory founded in 1488 (Gwynn and Hadcock 1970, 223; Conlan 2002, 224). The surviving architectural features, though fragmentary, are consistent with a late 15th-century construction date.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In a rath (SL039-085001-), immediately W of the entrance. A drystone-built beehive-shaped chamber (1.86m E-W; 1.65m N-S; H 1.25m) roofed by two large slabs. The chamber is open at N due to the collapse of a section of the roof. A creepway at the S side, topped by a lintel (L 0.84m; T 0.42m), leads into a passage. The passage continues to S for some distance, where it is open, and then turns to W. There is a possible second chamber at the W side, where a narrow aperture (Wth 0.32m) opens into the fosse of the rath.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).
